fullTitle: Practice Exam 1: AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer Associate (MLA-C01)

questions.promptHtml: An insurance claims analytics team is training an Amazon SageMaker AI built-in model on normalized, shuffled tabular data to flag suspicious claims. The fraud operations team requires the selected binary classifier to maintain a specified recall threshold and choose the model with the highest possible precision at that threshold. The ML engineer wants to use a built-in algorithm without writing custom training code. Which approach best meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An insurance claims analytics team is training an Amazon SageMaker AI built-in model on normalized, shuffled tabular data to flag suspicious claims. The fraud operations team requires the selected binary classifier to maintain a specified recall threshold and choose the model with the highest possible precision at that threshold. The ML engineer wants to use a built-in algorithm without writing custom training code.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Train Linear Learner with target_precision and recall_at_target_precision.
Train K-Means and classify claims by nearest cluster assignment.
Train XGBoost with eval_metric set to RMSE for model selection.
Train Linear Learner with target_recall and precision_at_target_recall.

correctText: Train Linear Learner with target_recall and precision_at_target_recall.
questions.explanationHtml:
Linear Learner is a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm for regression and classification on tabular data. For binary classification, it can train multiple candidate models and select among them according to criteria that reflect practical tradeoffs, such as precision versus recall. In this scenario, the operational requirement is not simply maximum overall accuracy, it is to keep recall at a required level and then maximize precision.

The correct mental model is that recall controls how many actual positive cases the model catches, while precision controls how many predicted positives are truly positive. Fraud and suspicious-claim workflows often care about recall because missing a true positive can be costly, but they also want high precision to avoid overwhelming reviewers with false alarms. Linear Learner's target_recall with precision_at_target_recall aligns directly with that tradeoff.

XGBoost is also a useful SageMaker built-in algorithm for tabular workloads, but choosing a generic metric such as RMSE does not express the required classification threshold behavior. K-Means solves a different type of problem, clustering unlabeled observations, so it is not the right fit when labeled suspicious and non-suspicious claims are available and a supervised binary classifier is needed. For more information, see the SageMaker AI built-in algorithms overview in Use Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithms or pretrained models and the tabular algorithm overview in Tabular data algorithms.

questions.promptHtml: A mobile gaming studio's analytics team is preparing player telemetry in Amazon S3 to train a churn prediction model. The data includes exact duplicate rows from ingestion retries, missing values in numeric session-duration fields, and unusually high purchase amounts that might skew training. The team wants to inspect these issues interactively, apply repeatable cleaning steps, and send the cleaned dataset to a machine learning workflow with the least custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A mobile gaming studio's analytics team is preparing player telemetry in Amazon S3 to train a churn prediction model. The data includes exact duplicate rows from ingestion retries, missing values in numeric session-duration fields, and unusually high purchase amounts that might skew training. The team wants to inspect these issues interactively, apply repeatable cleaning steps, and send the cleaned dataset to a machine learning workflow with the least custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run a SageMaker Data Wrangler data quality and insights report, add transforms for duplicate rows, missing values, and outliers, and export the flow for processing.
Enable Amazon Macie on the S3 bucket, review the sensitive data findings, and use the findings to prepare the training dataset.
Create an AWS Glue Data Catalog crawler, query the data with Amazon Athena, and train the model from the original S3 objects.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker endpoint, enable SageMaker Model Monitor, and use drift reports to correct the training dataset.

correctText: Run a SageMaker Data Wrangler data quality and insights report, add transforms for duplicate rows, missing values, and outliers, and export the flow for processing.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Data Wrangler is the best fit when an ML team needs to profile and transform data before training without writing a large amount of custom code. A data quality and insights report can help identify problems such as missing values, duplicate rows, anomalous samples, and outliers, while Data Wrangler transforms let the team define repeatable preparation steps for the dataset.

The mental model is that data preparation usually has two connected phases: first, inspect the data to understand quality problems, then encode the cleaning decisions as transformations that can be reused. For this scenario, that means detecting exact ingestion duplicates, deciding how to impute or remove missing numeric values, and treating outlier purchase amounts based on domain judgment rather than blindly feeding raw data to a model.

A Glue crawler and Athena are valuable for cataloging and querying data in S3, but a catalog alone does not clean the dataset. Macie addresses sensitive data discovery rather than general feature cleaning. SageMaker Model Monitor is important after deployment, but waiting until production monitoring to address known training data defects is an anti-pattern for data preparation.

For more information, see the SageMaker Data Wrangler transform reference at Transform data and the Data Wrangler data quality report reference at Get insights on data and data quality.

questions.promptHtml: A regional port authority's predictive maintenance team is preparing training data for a model that predicts crane component failures. Daily sensor events arrive as JSON files in Amazon S3, and maintenance work orders are stored in a JDBC-compatible relational database. The team must combine the records by crane ID and service date, apply basic cleansing, and write a curated Parquet dataset to Amazon S3 for downstream analytics and training. The team wants a repeatable managed pipeline with minimal infrastructure administration. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A regional port authority's predictive maintenance team is preparing training data for a model that predicts crane component failures. Daily sensor events arrive as JSON files in Amazon S3, and maintenance work orders are stored in a JDBC-compatible relational database. The team must combine the records by crane ID and service date, apply basic cleansing, and write a curated Parquet dataset to Amazon S3 for downstream analytics and training. The team wants a repeatable managed pipeline with minimal infrastructure administration.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Launch a long-running Amazon EMR cluster that runs a Spark job to read both sources, join the datasets, and write Parquet output to Amazon S3.
Build an AWS Glue Studio ETL job that reads both sources, joins the datasets on the matching keys, and writes Parquet output to Amazon S3.
Create a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow that imports both datasets, exports generated notebook code, and runs the notebook manually before training.
Export the work orders to Amazon S3, create Amazon Athena tables, run scheduled SQL joins, and store the query results as the training dataset.

correctText: Build an AWS Glue Studio ETL job that reads both sources, joins the datasets on the matching keys, and writes Parquet output to Amazon S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Glue is designed for managed extract, transform, and load workflows, including merging data from sources such as Amazon S3 and JDBC-connected databases. In this scenario, the team needs to join two datasets, perform basic cleansing, and produce a curated Parquet dataset in S3. AWS Glue Studio can define this kind of workflow visually, and the underlying managed Spark environment removes the need to provision and operate a separate cluster.

The relevant mental model is that AWS Glue is the production ETL service, while tools such as Athena, EMR, and SageMaker Data Wrangler are better suited to adjacent but different needs. Amazon EMR with Apache Spark is powerful for distributed processing, but it is a heavier operational choice when the requirement emphasizes minimal infrastructure administration. Amazon Athena is excellent for SQL exploration and querying S3 data, but using it as the primary ETL engine is a common anti-pattern when a managed transformation pipeline is needed.

SageMaker Data Wrangler is valuable for interactive ML-focused data preparation, visualization, and transformation experimentation. However, exported notebook code that is run manually is less appropriate than a managed AWS Glue ETL job for a repeatable pipeline. For documentation on Glue joins and data connections, see AWS Glue Studio Joining datasets and AWS Glue Connecting to data. For the EMR alternative, see Apache Spark on Amazon EMR.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A pharmaceutical research lab's ML platform team deploys Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints and container-based supporting resources for multiple research groups. The team needs repeatable deployments across development and production. The engineers prefer to define reusable infrastructure components in Python and want the deployment workflow to provision resources through AWS-managed stack operations. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom template maintenance?
questions.promptText:
A pharmaceutical research lab's ML platform team deploys Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints and container-based supporting resources for multiple research groups. The team needs repeatable deployments across development and production. The engineers prefer to define reusable infrastructure components in Python and want the deployment workflow to provision resources through AWS-managed stack operations.

Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom template maintenance?

options.text: Use SageMaker JumpStart to deploy each endpoint and record the deployed settings in a shared operations runbook.
Use AWS CDK constructs to define the resources in Python and synthesize the project to AWS CloudFormation stacks.
Use AWS CodeBuild to run shell scripts that call AWS CLI commands to create the endpoint resources.
Author AWS CloudFormation YAML templates directly and copy each template for every research group deployment.

correctText: Use AWS CDK constructs to define the resources in Python and synthesize the project to AWS CloudFormation stacks.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS CDK is designed for teams that want to define infrastructure by using familiar programming languages such as Python, TypeScript, Java, or .NET, then synthesize that code into CloudFormation templates. This makes it a good fit when engineers want reusable infrastructure components, higher-level abstractions, and repeatable deployments that still use AWS CloudFormation as the provisioning engine. See the AWS CDK overview and AWS CDK constructs.

AWS CloudFormation remains the underlying managed IaC service for modeling resources as stacks, applying stack updates, and tracking resource changes. Direct CloudFormation templates are appropriate when a team wants declarative YAML or JSON artifacts, but they can become harder to maintain when many similar deployments need reusable patterns. The CloudFormation workflow is described in the AWS CloudFormation overview and CloudFormation key concepts and workflow.

For ML deployment workflows, the key tradeoff is not whether CDK or CloudFormation can provision AWS resources, both can. The practical decision is whether the team wants direct declarative templates or a programming-language abstraction that produces those templates. In this scenario, the preference for Python and reusable components makes CDK the better fit, while SageMaker JumpStart and ad hoc CLI scripts do not provide the same IaC lifecycle for repeatable multi-environment deployments.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A renewable energy forecasting team hosts a regression model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Users report intermittent slow responses during peak request periods. The team needs to inspect application log messages from the endpoint and receive notifications when latency exceeds an acceptable threshold. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A renewable energy forecasting team hosts a regression model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Users report intermittent slow responses during peak request periods. The team needs to inspect application log messages from the endpoint and receive notifications when latency exceeds an acceptable threshold.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Config to evaluate endpoint configuration changes, and send compliance notifications to an SNS topic.
Use SageMaker Model Monitor to schedule drift checks, and review the generated reports in SageMaker Studio.
Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query endpoint logs, and create a CloudWatch alarm on endpoint latency metrics.
Use CloudTrail Insights to detect unusual endpoint activity, and create an EventBridge rule for insight events.

correctText: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query endpoint logs, and create a CloudWatch alarm on endpoint latency metrics.
questions.explanationHtml:
CloudWatch is the best fit when the task is operational troubleshooting of a SageMaker endpoint. SageMaker integrates with CloudWatch for endpoint metrics such as invocation activity and latency, and CloudWatch alarms can notify operators when a metric crosses a defined threshold. See the SageMaker monitoring overview in Monitor Amazon SageMaker AI and SageMaker metrics details in Monitor Amazon SageMaker AI with Amazon CloudWatch.

CloudWatch Logs Insights is used to search and analyze log data stored in CloudWatch Logs, which makes it suitable for investigating endpoint application messages, errors, and patterns around the time of latency spikes. It is an interactive query capability, not a replacement for metric alarms, so pairing it with a CloudWatch alarm gives both investigation and notification capabilities. For more information, see Analyze log data with CloudWatch Logs Insights and Using Amazon CloudWatch alarms.

CloudTrail, AWS Config, and SageMaker Model Monitor solve different problems. CloudTrail is for API auditing, AWS Config is for resource configuration history and compliance, and Model Monitor is for model and data quality monitoring. Those services can be valuable in an ML operations environment, but they do not provide the simplest path for querying endpoint logs and alarming on runtime latency.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A university climate science lab is onboarding data scientists to Amazon SageMaker AI. The data scientists need to run notebooks and training jobs that read approved training datasets from a single Amazon S3 bucket. The security team requires least-privilege access and does not want long-term AWS access keys stored in notebooks. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
questions.promptText:
A university climate science lab is onboarding data scientists to Amazon SageMaker AI. The data scientists need to run notebooks and training jobs that read approved training datasets from a single Amazon S3 bucket. The security team requires least-privilege access and does not want long-term AWS access keys stored in notebooks.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?

options.text: Use SageMaker Role Manager to create administrator IAM roles for all data scientists, and review SageMaker and S3 activity later in CloudTrail.
Add the data scientists to an IAM group with AmazonSageMakerFullAccess, and grant the group full access to the S3 bucket.
Create IAM access keys for each data scientist, and store the keys as environment variables in the SageMaker notebooks.
Use SageMaker Role Manager to create persona-based IAM roles with scoped S3 permissions, and allow users to pass only the approved SageMaker execution roles.

correctText: Use SageMaker Role Manager to create persona-based IAM roles with scoped S3 permissions, and allow users to pass only the approved SageMaker execution roles.
questions.explanationHtml:
IAM roles are the right control point when an AWS service needs to access another AWS service on behalf of a user or workload. In SageMaker AI, an execution role can grant only the permissions needed for the job, such as reading a specific S3 training prefix, instead of giving every data scientist broad direct access or requiring static credentials.

SageMaker Role Manager helps reduce setup effort by creating persona-based IAM roles for common ML activities. The role still should be scoped to the needed services and resources, and users should be allowed to pass only approved execution roles to SageMaker. The related IAM concept is iam:PassRole, which controls whether a principal can pass a role to an AWS service.

IAM groups are useful for assigning identity-based permissions to multiple users, but using broad managed policies or full bucket access does not satisfy least privilege. CloudTrail is important for auditability, but auditing after the fact is not a substitute for preventing unnecessary access in the first place.

For more information, see Amazon SageMaker Role Manager, SageMaker AI execution roles, IAM PassRole permissions, and IAM policy and permissions overview.

questions.promptHtml: An urban transit agency's analytics team is considering a custom ML model to forecast bus stop overcrowding one month ahead. The team has 3 months of route, ticketing, schedule, and weather data, but many records were manually corrected after service disruptions. A rules-based report that uses recent ridership already gives planners acceptable weekly guidance. The team wants to decide whether a custom ML solution is feasible before committing to a full training pipeline. Which action should the team take FIRST?
questions.promptText:
An urban transit agency's analytics team is considering a custom ML model to forecast bus stop overcrowding one month ahead. The team has 3 months of route, ticketing, schedule, and weather data, but many records were manually corrected after service disruptions. A rules-based report that uses recent ridership already gives planners acceptable weekly guidance. The team wants to decide whether a custom ML solution is feasible before committing to a full training pipeline.

Which action should the team take FIRST?

options.text: Build a custom deep learning model in SageMaker, tune multiple hyperparameters, and evaluate the model after the full pipeline is deployed.
Collect an additional year of operational data, store it in an S3 data lake, and postpone evaluation until all planned sources are available.
Define the forecast target and success metric, profile the available data, and compare a small prototype with the rules-based baseline.
Load all available records into SageMaker Autopilot, run an automated job, and accept the highest-ranked candidate from the leaderboard.

correctText: Define the forecast target and success metric, profile the available data, and compare a small prototype with the rules-based baseline.
questions.explanationHtml:
Before building a custom ML solution, an ML engineer should frame the work as a measurable prediction problem: identify the target variable, define evaluation metrics, inspect the available data, and compare a prototype against a simple baseline. This is especially important when an existing rules-based approach already produces acceptable results, because ML should improve a business outcome enough to justify the added cost, complexity, and maintenance.

In this scenario, the limited data history and manually corrected records are signals to perform data profiling and quality checks before committing to model training. A small prototype can test whether the available features contain enough predictive signal, while the rules-based report provides a baseline that any ML model should beat. AWS guidance on ML problem framing and determining whether ML is the right solution emphasizes this kind of feasibility evaluation.

Automated model building, deep learning, and larger data platforms can be valuable later, but they are not substitutes for problem framing and data assessment. The practical tradeoff is to spend a small amount of effort early to avoid a much larger investment in a model that lacks sufficient data, lacks a measurable target, or does not outperform a simpler alternative. Data quality preparation concepts are also covered in data preprocessing.

questions.promptHtml: A specialty grocer's demand analytics team has a CSV dataset with product, store, pricing, and promotion features. The target label indicates whether weekly demand exceeded a business threshold. Exploratory analysis shows feature interactions that are unlikely to be separated well by a simple linear boundary. The team wants to train in Amazon SageMaker AI with minimal custom container maintenance. Which approach should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A specialty grocer's demand analytics team has a CSV dataset with product, store, pricing, and promotion features. The target label indicates whether weekly demand exceeded a business threshold. Exploratory analysis shows feature interactions that are unlikely to be separated well by a simple linear boundary. The team wants to train in Amazon SageMaker AI with minimal custom container maintenance.

Which approach should the team use?

options.text: Train a SageMaker AI K-Means model and assign clusters to threshold classes.
Train a SageMaker AI built-in XGBoost model and tune tree-related hyperparameters.
Train a SageMaker AI image classification model and convert rows to tensors.
Train a SageMaker AI Linear Learner model and enable automatic normalization.

correctText: Train a SageMaker AI built-in XGBoost model and tune tree-related hyperparameters.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker AI built-in algorithms are intended to reduce operational overhead by providing managed training containers for common ML problem types. For a supervised tabular classification problem with nonlinear interactions, XGBoost is a strong fit because gradient-boosted decision trees can model interactions and nonlinear splits without requiring a custom training container.

Linear Learner is also a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm and can be appropriate for regression or classification when a linear relationship is sufficient. However, automatic normalization does not change the basic model family, so it does not address a scenario where the useful signal depends on nonlinear feature interactions. K-Means is unsupervised and image classification is for image data, so neither directly matches the labeled tabular classification task. For more information, see Use SageMaker AI built-in algorithms or pretrained models, Train a model with Amazon SageMaker AI, and XGBoost Algorithm.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A national retail bank's ML operations team has a fraud scoring model hosted on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has approved a new model version and wants to evaluate it with live production requests while limiting customer impact. The team must compare operational metrics and prediction behavior before routing most traffic to the new model, with minimal changes to the client application. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A national retail bank's ML operations team has a fraud scoring model hosted on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has approved a new model version and wants to evaluate it with live production requests while limiting customer impact. The team must compare operational metrics and prediction behavior before routing most traffic to the new model, with minimal changes to the client application.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the new model to a separate SageMaker endpoint, modify each client to select an endpoint, and compare application logs after all clients have been updated.
Run SageMaker batch transform with the new model against recent production requests, compare the outputs, and replace the real-time endpoint if the results are acceptable.
Enable SageMaker Model Monitor on the existing endpoint, configure a drift baseline, and automatically retrain the current model when CloudWatch alarms are triggered.
Update the SageMaker endpoint to host both model versions as production variants, route a small traffic percentage to the new version, and monitor CloudWatch metrics and captured inference data.

correctText: Update the SageMaker endpoint to host both model versions as production variants, route a small traffic percentage to the new version, and monitor CloudWatch metrics and captured inference data.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker production variants are the usual mechanism for controlled online comparison of model versions on a real-time endpoint. Each variant can host a different model version, and the endpoint can route a defined share of requests to each variant. This supports an A/B style rollout because the client can continue invoking the same endpoint while SageMaker handles the traffic distribution.

For production evaluation, the team should combine controlled traffic routing with observability. Amazon CloudWatch provides endpoint metrics such as invocation and latency metrics, and SageMaker data capture can record inputs and inference outputs to Amazon S3 for monitoring, debugging, and later analysis. If ground truth labels become available, model quality monitoring can compare predictions against those labels to help determine whether the new model is performing acceptably.

Deploying a separate endpoint and changing clients can work in simple experiments, but it pushes routing logic into applications and increases the chance of inconsistent rollout behavior. Batch transform is an offline inference pattern, so it does not validate the new model under live request patterns. Model Monitor is valuable for drift and quality monitoring, but it is not a replacement for a controlled deployment strategy that sends a limited percentage of production traffic to the new model.

For more information, see Test models in production, Model validation, Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch, and Capture data from deployed models.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A maritime logistics team has packaged a custom data validation service as a Docker image. The service runs as a stateless container in an ML workflow, processes files from Amazon S3, and writes validated outputs back to Amazon S3. The team wants to run multiple copies during peak workloads but does not want to provision or patch container hosts. The team does not use Kubernetes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A maritime logistics team has packaged a custom data validation service as a Docker image. The service runs as a stateless container in an ML workflow, processes files from Amazon S3, and writes validated outputs back to Amazon S3. The team wants to run multiple copies during peak workloads but does not want to provision or patch container hosts. The team does not use Kubernetes.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Push the image to Amazon ECR, create an Amazon EKS workload, and run the service on managed node groups.
Push the image to Amazon ECR, create an Amazon ECS task definition, and run the service on EC2 launch type.
Push the image to Amazon ECR, create an Amazon ECS task definition, and run the service on AWS Fargate.
Package the image as a SageMaker AI model, create a real-time endpoint, and scale endpoint instances.

correctText: Push the image to Amazon ECR, create an Amazon ECS task definition, and run the service on AWS Fargate.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate is the best fit when a team already has a Docker container and wants AWS to run it without managing the underlying container hosts. The team defines how the task should run, including the image, CPU, memory, networking, logging, and IAM settings, and Fargate provides the serverless compute capacity for the tasks.

Amazon ECR is the managed registry service used to store container images that ECS tasks can pull at runtime. An Amazon ECS task definition acts as the blueprint for the container workload, while an ECS service can keep the desired number of task copies running and can be adjusted for peak workloads.

The EC2 launch type for ECS is still valid, but it requires managing the EC2 instances that provide cluster capacity. Amazon EKS is a strong choice for teams that have standardized on Kubernetes, but it is unnecessary when the requirement is simply to run containers with minimal overhead and no Kubernetes dependency. SageMaker AI containers are important for ML training and inference, but a generic validation service is better matched to a container orchestration service.

For more information, see Amazon ECS overview, AWS Fargate for Amazon ECS, Amazon ECS task definitions, and Amazon ECR overview.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A digital pathology lab has trained an image classification model and saved the model artifacts in Amazon S3. The lab needs to serve individual predictions to a web application with low latency during business hours. The ML team wants managed model hosting, autoscaling, and controlled rollout options for future model versions. The team does not want to operate a general-purpose container orchestration platform. Which deployment target best meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A digital pathology lab has trained an image classification model and saved the model artifacts in Amazon S3. The lab needs to serve individual predictions to a web application with low latency during business hours. The ML team wants managed model hosting, autoscaling, and controlled rollout options for future model versions. The team does not want to operate a general-purpose container orchestration platform.

Which deployment target best meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the model to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint.
Deploy the model as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate.
Deploy the model as an AWS Lambda container image function.
Deploy the model as Pods on an Amazon EKS cluster.

correctText: Deploy the model to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker AI real-time inference is the best fit when an ML model must serve individual predictions to an application with low latency. SageMaker AI manages the model hosting environment and supports endpoint capabilities that are specific to ML operations, including endpoint scaling and controlled deployment patterns for new model versions. See SageMaker AI real-time inference endpoints and SageMaker AI model deployment workflow and inference options.

General-purpose container platforms are useful, but they optimize for a different tradeoff. Amazon EKS is a strong choice when an organization already wants Kubernetes abstractions such as Pods, Services, and Kubernetes autoscaling, especially for teams standardizing on Kubernetes across environments. Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate reduces server management for containers, but the team would still own more of the model serving, deployment, and ML-specific operational logic than with SageMaker AI.

AWS Lambda can package dependencies in a container image and can be useful for event-driven inference tasks, but it is not the best match for a managed low-latency model endpoint with rollout guardrails. The exam pattern to recognize is that low-latency, individual predictions with ML-specific hosting requirements usually point to a SageMaker AI endpoint, while Kubernetes or ECS are better when the primary requirement is container orchestration rather than managed ML hosting. For container-oriented alternatives, see Amazon EKS workload deployment concepts, Amazon ECS task definitions, and AWS Lambda container image deployment requirements.

questions.promptHtml: A wildlife conservation nonprofit's ML team is evaluating a binary classification model that flags drone images that may contain injured animals. Missing an image that actually contains an injured animal has the highest operational impact. The team also wants to compare candidate models across several classification thresholds before choosing a threshold for production. Which TWO actions should the team take to analyze model performance?
questions.promptText:
A wildlife conservation nonprofit's ML team is evaluating a binary classification model that flags drone images that may contain injured animals. Missing an image that actually contains an injured animal has the highest operational impact. The team also wants to compare candidate models across several classification thresholds before choosing a threshold for production.

Which TWO actions should the team take to analyze model performance?

options.text: Calculate precision from the confusion matrix to prioritize reducing missed injured-animal images.
Compare RMSE and MAE values to evaluate classification errors across candidate models.
Plot ROC curves and compare AUC values to evaluate threshold tradeoffs across models.
Calculate recall from the confusion matrix to quantify missed injured-animal images.
Use a data quality baseline in Model Monitor to replace threshold analysis before deployment.

correctText: Plot ROC curves and compare AUC values to evaluate threshold tradeoffs across models.
Calculate recall from the confusion matrix to quantify missed injured-animal images.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a binary classifier, a confusion matrix separates predictions into true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives. When the main business risk is missing an actual positive case, the most relevant metric is recall, calculated as true positives / (true positives + false negatives). In this scenario, a false negative means an image that contains an injured animal was not flagged.

ROC curves are useful when the model produces scores and the team has not yet chosen a classification threshold. The curve shows how the true positive rate changes relative to the false positive rate as the threshold changes, and AUC provides a single summary value for comparing candidate models. The final threshold still requires operational judgment, because a higher recall setting can increase false positives.

Precision is not wrong as a general classification metric, but it answers a different question: how many flagged images are actually positive. Regression metrics such as RMSE and MAE are appropriate when predicting continuous numeric values, not when analyzing a binary classification model. SageMaker Model Monitor can help in production, especially with model quality monitoring when ground-truth labels are available, but a data quality baseline is not a substitute for predeployment classifier performance analysis.

Relevant AWS documentation includes SageMaker Autopilot model-performance metrics, SageMaker Autopilot model insights, and SageMaker Model Monitor model quality monitoring.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A live sports analytics group hosts a player injury risk model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Request volume is low most of the week, increases sharply during scheduled games, and sometimes spikes further during overtime. The team wants endpoint capacity to increase before known game windows and still adjust automatically when unexpected traffic occurs. The team wants to minimize manual threshold tuning. Which scaling approach should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A live sports analytics group hosts a player injury risk model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Request volume is low most of the week, increases sharply during scheduled games, and sometimes spikes further during overtime. The team wants endpoint capacity to increase before known game windows and still adjust automatically when unexpected traffic occurs. The team wants to minimize manual threshold tuning.

Which scaling approach should the team use?

options.text: Configure only scheduled scaling actions that set endpoint capacity before and after each game window.
Configure only a step scaling policy that changes endpoint capacity at several CloudWatch alarm thresholds.
Configure scheduled scaling for game windows and add a target tracking scaling policy for runtime traffic changes.
Configure only a larger fixed instance count for the endpoint variant before the season begins.

correctText: Configure scheduled scaling for game windows and add a target tracking scaling policy for runtime traffic changes.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker AI real-time endpoints, Application Auto Scaling can adjust the number of instances behind an endpoint variant as traffic changes. When demand has both a predictable component and an unpredictable component, a practical design is to combine scheduled scaling with a reactive policy such as target tracking.

Scheduled scaling is useful for known business events because it changes capacity proactively, before load arrives. Target tracking is useful when the team wants the scaling system to maintain a chosen utilization level without defining several separate threshold bands. Step scaling is still valid for cases that need precise alarm-driven adjustments, but it usually requires more tuning than target tracking. Keeping a fixed endpoint fleet is simpler, but it trades away cost efficiency and does not adapt well to changing traffic.

See the SageMaker AI endpoint scaling guidance in SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling overview, the Application Auto Scaling overview in Application Auto Scaling concepts, and the scheduled scaling behavior in Scheduled scaling for Application Auto Scaling.

questions.promptHtml: A documentary streaming service's ML team trains a personalization model on several terabytes of sequential training records stored in Amazon S3. The team uses an Amazon SageMaker AI training job with the default S3 input behavior, and each run spends a long time staging the full dataset before the training script starts. The team wants to reduce training startup time with the least data movement and the least operational change. Which solution will best meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A documentary streaming service's ML team trains a personalization model on several terabytes of sequential training records stored in Amazon S3. The team uses an Amazon SageMaker AI training job with the default S3 input behavior, and each run spends a long time staging the full dataset before the training script starts. The team wants to reduce training startup time with the least data movement and the least operational change.

Which solution will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on the training data bucket.
Increase the SageMaker AI training job's local storage volume size.
Copy the training dataset to Amazon EFS and mount it in the training job.
Configure the SageMaker AI training input channel to use S3 Fast File mode.

correctText: Configure the SageMaker AI training input channel to use S3 Fast File mode.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker AI training jobs, the input mode controls how training data is made available to the training container. The default File mode downloads data from Amazon S3 to local storage before training starts, which can create long startup delays for large datasets. Fast File mode provides file-system style access to S3 data so the training script can start sooner, and it works best for workloads that read data sequentially.

Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration solves a different problem: accelerating long-distance PUT and GET transfers through special S3 endpoints. It does not make a SageMaker AI training job stop staging the full dataset when the job is still configured for File mode. Amazon EFS and larger local training storage can be valid choices for other workload requirements, but they do not meet the stated need as directly because they add data placement or capacity considerations instead of changing how SageMaker AI reads existing S3 training data.

See the SageMaker AI documentation on training data access in Access Training Data. For related storage options, see Getting started with Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration and Amazon EFS performance.

questions.promptHtml: An aerospace maintenance analytics team stores aircraft inspection records as CSV files in Amazon S3. Before training a tabular failure prediction model, the team must visually inspect feature distributions, remove duplicate records, convert a numeric field that was imported as a string, and encode categorical fields. The team wants to perform these tasks with the least custom code and keep the preparation steps reusable. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An aerospace maintenance analytics team stores aircraft inspection records as CSV files in Amazon S3. Before training a tabular failure prediction model, the team must visually inspect feature distributions, remove duplicate records, convert a numeric field that was imported as a string, and encode categorical fields. The team wants to perform these tasks with the least custom code and keep the preparation steps reusable.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to import and visualize the files, apply built-in transforms, and export the data flow.
Use AWS Glue Data Quality to define rulesets, review data quality scores, and write an ETL script for the transformations.
Use Amazon Athena to query the S3 files, create transformed tables, and maintain SQL statements for the preparation logic.
Use Amazon SageMaker Feature Store to create feature groups, load the raw records, and reuse the stored features for training.

correctText: Use Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to import and visualize the files, apply built-in transforms, and export the data flow.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler is the best fit when an ML team needs to inspect and prepare data for modeling with minimal custom code. It provides a visual workflow for importing data, visualizing it, and applying transformations such as type conversion, duplicate handling, and categorical encoding. Exporting the data flow helps make the preparation steps repeatable instead of leaving them as one-off manual work.

A useful mental model is that Data Wrangler is optimized for the prepare and featurize stage of an ML workflow, while services such as Athena and Glue are broader data engineering tools. Athena is powerful for SQL queries over S3 data, but the team would need to build and maintain much of the preparation logic manually. AWS Glue Data Quality can evaluate data against rules and is valuable in ETL pipelines, but the scenario asks for an interactive, low-code way to inspect and transform data for modeling.

SageMaker Feature Store becomes valuable after features are curated because it helps store and share feature definitions for training, batch inference, and real-time inference. Loading raw, unprepared records into a feature store does not address the immediate need to visualize, clean, convert, and encode the data. For this scenario, the practical sequence is to prepare the raw data first, then store reusable features if they will be shared across models or inference workflows.

For more information, see SageMaker Data Wrangler overview, Data Wrangler transform reference, AWS Glue Data Quality overview, and SageMaker Feature Store.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A pharmaceutical research platform team stores trained model artifacts and validation datasets in an Amazon S3 bucket. The team must retain an audit record for more than 90 days that shows object-level activity on the bucket, including reads, uploads, and deletes. The team also wants to query the audit logs later during investigations. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A pharmaceutical research platform team stores trained model artifacts and validation datasets in an Amazon S3 bucket. The team must retain an audit record for more than 90 days that shows object-level activity on the bucket, including reads, uploads, and deletes. The team also wants to query the audit logs later during investigations.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS Config recorder that tracks the bucket and sends configuration change notifications to Amazon SNS.
Create a CloudTrail trail that logs management write events for the account and delivers the logs to Amazon S3.
Enable Amazon S3 request metrics for the bucket and create a CloudWatch dashboard to graph request activity.
Create a CloudTrail trail that logs S3 object-level data events for the bucket and delivers the logs to Amazon S3.

correctText: Create a CloudTrail trail that logs S3 object-level data events for the bucket and delivers the logs to Amazon S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS CloudTrail records API activity in an AWS account. CloudTrail event history is useful for recent investigation, but trails are the mechanism used when logs must be delivered to durable storage such as Amazon S3 for longer retention and later analysis. For setup guidance, see Overview of creating trails.

The important distinction in this scenario is between management events and data events. Management events are logged by trails by default and cover operations performed on resources, such as IAM policy changes or subnet creation. S3 object-level operations, including GetObject, PutObject, and DeleteObject, are data events and must be explicitly selected because they can be high volume. The event selector behavior is described in CloudTrail EventSelector.

For an ML platform, model artifacts and validation datasets often need stronger auditability than ordinary operational metrics provide. A trail that delivers S3 data events to an S3 bucket creates an auditable log source that can later be queried, for example with Athena, without relying on the limited event history view. If using a dedicated log bucket, the bucket policy must allow CloudTrail to deliver logs, as described in Amazon S3 bucket policy for CloudTrail.

questions.promptHtml: A university admissions analytics team exports several years of applicant records to Amazon S3 for a binary classification model that predicts whether admitted applicants will enroll. The CSV file is sorted by export date. Initial profiling shows that one socioeconomic facet has far fewer records and a lower positive-label proportion than other facets. The team wants to prepare the data before training to reduce prediction bias while keeping validation and test results meaningful for unseen applicants. Which approach should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A university admissions analytics team exports several years of applicant records to Amazon S3 for a binary classification model that predicts whether admitted applicants will enroll. The CSV file is sorted by export date. Initial profiling shows that one socioeconomic facet has far fewer records and a lower positive-label proportion than other facets. The team wants to prepare the data before training to reduce prediction bias while keeping validation and test results meaningful for unseen applicants.

Which approach should the team use?

options.text: Remove the facet columns before splitting the data, train on random records, and evaluate without checking label distribution.
Use SageMaker Data Wrangler to split the data by date, rebalance validation records, and leave underrepresented training records unchanged.
Oversample underrepresented records before splitting the data, train on the training split, and evaluate on the resulting test set.
Create a combined label-and-facet column, use SageMaker Data Wrangler to shuffle and stratified-split on that column, and augment only underrepresented training records.

correctText: Create a combined label-and-facet column, use SageMaker Data Wrangler to shuffle and stratified-split on that column, and augment only underrepresented training records.
questions.explanationHtml:
Bias reduction during data preparation is about controlling what the model learns from, while preserving an honest way to measure whether the model generalizes. For a dataset that is sorted by an operational artifact such as export date, shuffling helps avoid accidental train, validation, and test splits that reflect file order instead of the population. When the goal is to preserve representation across both the target label and a fairness-relevant facet, a practical approach is to create a single combined stratification column and split on that column.

Augmentation or oversampling should generally be applied to the training portion only. If synthetic or duplicated records are also placed into validation or test data, the evaluation can become easier or less realistic, which weakens confidence that the model will behave well on new applicants. The validation and test sets should remain a meaningful proxy for unseen data, while the training set can be adjusted to reduce the effect of underrepresented groups or labels.

Amazon SageMaker data preparation guidance includes tasks such as assessing and mitigating bias and splitting data for training and testing, as described in Overview of SageMaker AI data preparation options. SageMaker Data Wrangler provides transforms for operations such as shuffling, sampling, and splitting data, as described in Data Wrangler transform reference. SageMaker Clarify can help identify pre-training bias in raw datasets before model training, as described in SageMaker Clarify pre-training data bias overview.

questions.promptHtml: An energy trading desk trained a PyTorch price forecasting model on premises. The team saved the trained model artifact and has custom Python preprocessing and inference code that must run with each prediction. The team wants to host the existing model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint without re-training the model. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An energy trading desk trained a PyTorch price forecasting model on premises. The team saved the trained model artifact and has custom Python preprocessing and inference code that must run with each prediction. The team wants to host the existing model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint without re-training the model.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Convert the artifact to a SageMaker built-in algorithm format, retrain the model in a SageMaker training job, create a SageMaker model, and deploy an endpoint.
Package the inference code in a SageMaker-compatible Docker image, push the image to Amazon ECR, upload the model artifact to Amazon S3, create a SageMaker model, and deploy an endpoint.
Upload the artifact to Amazon S3, create a SageMaker model with an AWS-provided PyTorch inference image, create an endpoint configuration, and deploy an endpoint.
Register the artifact and container image in SageMaker Model Registry, approve the model package, and stop the release workflow after approval.

correctText: Package the inference code in a SageMaker-compatible Docker image, push the image to Amazon ECR, upload the model artifact to Amazon S3, create a SageMaker model, and deploy an endpoint.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a model that was trained outside SageMaker AI, the practical integration pattern is to separate the model artifact from the inference runtime. The trained artifact is stored in Amazon S3, and the code and dependencies that know how to load the artifact and respond to prediction requests are packaged in a container image, commonly stored in Amazon ECR. SageMaker AI then creates a model resource from those pieces and deploys that model to an endpoint for real-time inference.

This design is why SageMaker AI can host models that were not trained by SageMaker AI. The service does not require that training occurred in SageMaker, but it does require a deployable inference environment that follows the hosting contract. The documentation for deploying models describes the relationship among model artifacts, inference images, model resources, endpoint configurations, and endpoints in Deploy models for real-time inference, and the custom container contract is described in Use your own inference code with hosting services.

Model Registry is useful for versioning, approvals, and governance, but it is not a runtime serving layer. Similarly, retraining with a built-in algorithm can be useful in other scenarios, and AWS-provided framework images can be useful when they include the needed serving logic, but neither approach satisfies the requirement to preserve an existing externally trained model while running the team's custom inference code.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A regional ambulance dispatch service hosts a triage-priority model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. During large public events, request volume increases quickly and operators report slower responses. The ML operations team needs to monitor infrastructure performance and automatically add endpoint capacity when traffic grows. The team does not need to evaluate model bias or data drift for this requirement. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A regional ambulance dispatch service hosts a triage-priority model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. During large public events, request volume increases quickly and operators report slower responses. The ML operations team needs to monitor infrastructure performance and automatically add endpoint capacity when traffic grows. The team does not need to evaluate model bias or data drift for this requirement.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor schedules for data quality. Configure retraining when feature statistics deviate from the baseline.
Create CloudWatch alarms and dashboards for endpoint invocations, latency, errors, and host utilization. Configure SageMaker endpoint auto scaling.
Enable CloudTrail Insights for the account. Configure EventBridge to redeploy the endpoint when unusual write activity is detected.
Create AWS Config rules for the endpoint resources. Configure SNS notifications when endpoint configuration drift is detected.

correctText: Create CloudWatch alarms and dashboards for endpoint invocations, latency, errors, and host utilization. Configure SageMaker endpoint auto scaling.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a production SageMaker real-time endpoint, infrastructure monitoring should focus on signals such as request volume, latency, error behavior, and host-level utilization. These metrics help the team understand whether the endpoint is overloaded, whether responses are slowing down, and whether more capacity is needed.

Amazon CloudWatch is the primary service for collecting SageMaker endpoint metrics, creating dashboards, and configuring alarms. SageMaker endpoint auto scaling uses CloudWatch metrics to adjust endpoint capacity within configured scaling limits, which fits workloads that experience changing traffic patterns. See the SageMaker CloudWatch metrics documentation at Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch and the auto scaling policy documentation at Automatically scale SageMaker models.

CloudTrail, AWS Config, and SageMaker Model Monitor are valuable, but they address different operational questions. CloudTrail answers who called which API and when, AWS Config tracks configuration and compliance changes, and SageMaker Model Monitor evaluates production data and model behavior such as drift. None of those services is the best primary mechanism for scaling endpoint capacity based on inference workload performance.

questions.promptHtml: A specialty grocery chain's analytics team is building two separate models in Amazon SageMaker. The first model must predict a numeric weekly inventory demand value from labeled tabular records that include sales, promotions, and local event indicators. The second model must discover natural groups of stores from unlabeled numeric behavior data so the merchandising team can analyze store segments. The team wants to use built-in algorithms suited to each problem type. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A specialty grocery chain's analytics team is building two separate models in Amazon SageMaker. The first model must predict a numeric weekly inventory demand value from labeled tabular records that include sales, promotions, and local event indicators. The second model must discover natural groups of stores from unlabeled numeric behavior data so the merchandising team can analyze store segments. The team wants to use built-in algorithms suited to each problem type.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Train a SageMaker K-Means model to predict weekly demand from the labeled tabular features.
Train a SageMaker Linear Learner model to discover store segments from the unlabeled behavior features.
Train a SageMaker K-Means model to cluster stores from the unlabeled behavior features.
Train a SageMaker PCA model to produce weekly demand predictions from the labeled tabular features.
Train a SageMaker XGBoost model to predict weekly demand from the labeled tabular features.

correctText: Train a SageMaker K-Means model to cluster stores from the unlabeled behavior features.
Train a SageMaker XGBoost model to predict weekly demand from the labeled tabular features.
questions.explanationHtml:
The two workloads require different mental models. Predicting a numeric target from examples that already contain historical outcomes is a supervised regression problem, so a tabular supervised algorithm such as XGBoost is appropriate. Discovering store groups without target labels is an unsupervised clustering problem, so K-Means fits the segmentation requirement.

SageMaker provides different built-in algorithms for different problem families, and choosing the algorithm starts with identifying whether the data has labels and what the desired output should be. The SageMaker algorithm overview maps common problem types to built-in algorithms, including tabular supervised algorithms and unsupervised algorithms. See Use Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithms or pretrained models, XGBoost Algorithm, and Unsupervised Learning Algorithms.

The distractors confuse adjacent algorithm categories. Linear Learner can be a good supervised choice for regression or classification, but it is not an unlabeled clustering algorithm. K-Means and PCA are useful unsupervised tools, but K-Means clusters records and PCA reduces dimensionality, neither one directly learns a labeled regression target such as weekly demand.

questions.promptHtml: A global apparel marketplace's demand forecasting team stores several terabytes of product view and purchase events in Amazon S3 as newline-delimited JSON. Data scientists use Amazon Athena to explore the data and build ML feature datasets. Most queries scan many days of events but read only a small set of fields, such as product_id, category, price, and event_time. The team wants to reduce query cost and improve query performance without moving the data out of Amazon S3. Which solution will best meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A global apparel marketplace's demand forecasting team stores several terabytes of product view and purchase events in Amazon S3 as newline-delimited JSON. Data scientists use Amazon Athena to explore the data and build ML feature datasets. Most queries scan many days of events but read only a small set of fields, such as product_id, category, price, and event_time. The team wants to reduce query cost and improve query performance without moving the data out of Amazon S3.

Which solution will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Keep the curated event dataset as JSON files in Amazon S3.
Convert the curated event dataset to Parquet files in Amazon S3.
Convert the curated event dataset to CSV files in Amazon S3.
Convert the curated event dataset to Avro files in Amazon S3.

correctText: Convert the curated event dataset to Parquet files in Amazon S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
For analytics over large datasets in Amazon S3, the access pattern should drive the file format decision. When queries commonly read only a few fields across many records, a columnar format such as Parquet is usually a better fit than row-oriented text formats because the query engine can focus on the referenced columns instead of reading entire records.

CSV and JSON are valuable interchange formats because they are simple and widely supported, and JSON is especially useful for semi-structured data. However, they are text-based formats and are less efficient when the workload repeatedly performs analytical scans over selected fields. Avro is compact and useful when schema evolution and serialization are important, but it is not the strongest match for column-pruning analytics.

Amazon Athena charges based on the amount of data scanned, so reducing unnecessary reads can improve both performance and cost. AWS guidance for Athena discusses using columnar formats such as Parquet and ORC for this kind of workload in Use columnar storage formats, and AWS Glue supports common ETL input and output formats as described in Format options for ETL inputs and outputs in AWS Glue.

questions.promptHtml: A municipal water treatment operations team is building a model to flag whether a pump will need maintenance in the next 7 days. The team has a few hundred thousand rows of structured maintenance records in Amazon S3. The target is binary. Initial experiments show that a simple tabular model meets the required recall target, and the team wants the lowest-cost approach to retrain weekly and serve low-volume predictions. Which approach should the team choose?
questions.promptText:
A municipal water treatment operations team is building a model to flag whether a pump will need maintenance in the next 7 days. The team has a few hundred thousand rows of structured maintenance records in Amazon S3. The target is binary. Initial experiments show that a simple tabular model meets the required recall target, and the team wants the lowest-cost approach to retrain weekly and serve low-volume predictions.

Which approach should the team choose?

options.text: Run SageMaker Autopilot in HPO mode and accept the highest-ranked candidate after all trials complete.
Train a custom PyTorch deep neural network on GPU instances and tune the network depth and dropout rate.
Fine-tune a SageMaker JumpStart foundation model and host it behind a persistent real-time endpoint.
Train a SageMaker built-in Linear Learner binary classifier on CPU instances and tune only the necessary hyperparameters.

correctText: Train a SageMaker built-in Linear Learner binary classifier on CPU instances and tune only the necessary hyperparameters.
questions.explanationHtml:
When cost is a primary constraint, start with the simplest model that meets the business metric, then add complexity only when evaluation results justify it. In this scenario, the data is structured and tabular, the prediction target is binary, and earlier experiments already meet the required recall target, so a managed built-in algorithm such as Linear Learner is a better fit than deep learning or foundation model fine-tuning.

SageMaker built-in algorithms reduce the need to package and maintain custom training containers, and they can run on appropriately sized training infrastructure. The SageMaker documentation describes how to choose among pretrained models, built-in algorithms, framework code, and custom containers in Choose an algorithm, and maps common use cases to built-in options in Use SageMaker built-in algorithms or pretrained models.

Cost is not only about the algorithm itself. It is also affected by the number of training jobs, the instance family, the use of accelerators, and whether endpoints sit idle. SageMaker training guidance covers selecting instance types and cost-saving options in Train a model with Amazon SageMaker, while inference cost tradeoffs are discussed in Optimize your inference costs using Amazon SageMaker.

questions.promptHtml: A wildlife conservation consortium's ML team is preparing a training dataset in Amazon S3 for a binary classification model. The records include numeric sensor readings, ranger note text, and image-derived categorical tags. The team already has access to Amazon SageMaker Clarify and wants a pre-training report that checks whether the training records are distributed unevenly across two values of the survey_region facet, without evaluating differences in positive-label rates. Which action will meet this requirement?
questions.promptText:
A wildlife conservation consortium's ML team is preparing a training dataset in Amazon S3 for a binary classification model. The records include numeric sensor readings, ranger note text, and image-derived categorical tags. The team already has access to Amazon SageMaker Clarify and wants a pre-training report that checks whether the training records are distributed unevenly across two values of the survey_region facet, without evaluating differences in positive-label rates.

Which action will meet this requirement?

options.text: Configure a SageMaker Clarify pre-training analysis to calculate Class Imbalance for the survey_region facet.
Configure a SageMaker Clarify pre-training analysis to calculate Difference in Proportions of Labels for the survey_region facet.
Configure a SageMaker Clarify pre-training analysis to calculate Kullback-Leibler Divergence for the survey_region facet.
Configure SageMaker Model Monitor to create a model quality baseline for the survey_region facet.

correctText: Configure a SageMaker Clarify pre-training analysis to calculate Class Imbalance for the survey_region facet.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics are used to examine raw training data before a model is trained. In this scenario, the team is asking whether examples are unevenly distributed across values of a facet, so Class Imbalance is the matching metric. The stem states that the organization already has access to SageMaker Clarify, so using Clarify is a valid action for this scenario.

Difference in Proportions of Labels answers a different question: whether positive labels occur at different rates for different facet values. That can be important for fairness analysis, but it depends on label outcomes, which the requirement explicitly excludes. Distribution-based metrics such as Kullback-Leibler Divergence are also pre-training metrics, but they focus on divergence in outcome distributions rather than the simpler question of whether one facet has fewer examples.

The practical mental model is to separate who is represented in the dataset from what labels those groups receive. Use Class Imbalance for representation across facet values, and use Difference in Proportions of Labels when the positive-label rate itself is the concern. For more detail, see Amazon SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics, Class Imbalance, and Difference in Proportions of Labels.

questions.promptHtml: A precision agriculture cooperative's ML team retrains a crop disease risk model every month in Amazon SageMaker. Auditors require the team to identify which model artifact, training dataset, training job, validation metrics, approval decision, and deployed endpoint were associated with each production release. The team wants to meet these requirements with the least custom tracking code. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A precision agriculture cooperative's ML team retrains a crop disease risk model every month in Amazon SageMaker. Auditors require the team to identify which model artifact, training dataset, training job, validation metrics, approval decision, and deployed endpoint were associated with each production release. The team wants to meet these requirements with the least custom tracking code.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Use SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking to associate datasets, training jobs, artifacts, models, and endpoints.
Use SageMaker Feature Store to save model artifacts and retrieve the approved artifact during deployment.
Register each release in a SageMaker Model Registry model package group with metrics, metadata, and approval status.
Store each model artifact in an Amazon S3 prefix that includes the training date and validation score.
Use SageMaker Experiments to compare trial results and treat the best trial as the production version.

correctText: Use SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking to associate datasets, training jobs, artifacts, models, and endpoints.
Register each release in a SageMaker Model Registry model package group with metrics, metadata, and approval status.
questions.explanationHtml:
For auditability, the team needs both a versioned model catalog and a way to trace how each version was produced and deployed. SageMaker Model Registry provides the managed catalog layer: model package groups contain model versions, and each version can include metadata, metrics, and an approval state that supports controlled promotion to production. See the SageMaker Model Registry overview and Model Registry model versions documentation.

SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking complements the registry by recording relationships among datasets, processing or training jobs, model artifacts, models, and endpoints. That lineage is what lets an engineer answer audit questions such as, which data and training run produced the endpoint currently serving production traffic? For this purpose, see SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking.

Using S3 naming conventions or experiment names can help with informal organization, but those approaches put the burden on custom processes and manual discipline. SageMaker Experiments is valuable during development, while Feature Store is valuable for feature consistency, but neither is the managed production model version and approval system required here.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A digital publishing platform's recommendations team maintains an Amazon SageMaker model that is deployed to a real-time endpoint. The team wants commits to a model repository to start a repeatable workflow that builds artifacts, preprocesses data, trains the model, evaluates the model, registers the model version, deploys to a staging endpoint, and requires approval before production deployment. The team wants to minimize custom orchestration code while maintaining CI/CD traceability. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A digital publishing platform's recommendations team maintains an Amazon SageMaker model that is deployed to a real-time endpoint. The team wants commits to a model repository to start a repeatable workflow that builds artifacts, preprocesses data, trains the model, evaluates the model, registers the model version, deploys to a staging endpoint, and requires approval before production deployment. The team wants to minimize custom orchestration code while maintaining CI/CD traceability.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function that starts SageMaker training jobs and updates the production endpoint.
Create an AWS CodePipeline workflow that runs all preprocessing, training, and evaluation logic inside CodeBuild and then updates the endpoint.
Build an Amazon MWAA DAG that runs SageMaker jobs, evaluates the output, and calls endpoint deployment APIs after each successful run.
Create an Amazon SageMaker Project from an MLOps template, define the workflow with SageMaker Pipelines, and use CodePipeline and CodeBuild for staged deployment.

correctText: Create an Amazon SageMaker Project from an MLOps template, define the workflow with SageMaker Pipelines, and use CodePipeline and CodeBuild for staged deployment.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Projects are designed for native MLOps workflows in SageMaker Studio, including CI/CD patterns that use code repositories, SageMaker Pipelines, CodeBuild, and CodePipeline. In this scenario, the workflow needs more than a single training job: it needs repeatable preprocessing, training, evaluation, model registration, staged deployment, and approval before production.

SageMaker Pipelines provides a managed way to define ML workflow steps as a directed workflow, such as processing, training, evaluation, and model registration. CodePipeline and CodeBuild can then automate the build and deployment portions of the release process, which gives the team CI/CD traceability without writing a custom orchestration framework. See Define a pipeline and SageMaker Projects MLOps templates.

EventBridge is useful for event-driven automation, including triggering pipeline executions or responding to SageMaker state changes, but using it only to invoke Lambda functions shifts orchestration responsibility to custom code. MWAA is also a valid workflow orchestrator, but for a SageMaker-centered CI/CD workflow with minimal custom orchestration, the managed SageMaker Projects and Pipelines approach is the better fit. For related event-driven integration patterns, see Schedule or trigger a pipeline with Amazon EventBridge.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A seaport authority's cargo analytics team trains an Amazon SageMaker model to estimate inspection priority for shipping containers. Each night, an upstream system writes a CSV file with all containers scheduled for the next day to Amazon S3. The team must generate predictions for the complete file before morning planning begins. No application needs individual predictions during the day, and the operations team wants to avoid paying for idle hosting capacity. Which deployment option best meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A seaport authority's cargo analytics team trains an Amazon SageMaker model to estimate inspection priority for shipping containers. Each night, an upstream system writes a CSV file with all containers scheduled for the next day to Amazon S3. The team must generate predictions for the complete file before morning planning begins. No application needs individual predictions during the day, and the operations team wants to avoid paying for idle hosting capacity.

Which deployment option best meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the model to an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint and invoke it once for each row in the file.
Run an Amazon SageMaker Batch Transform job against the nightly S3 input file and write predictions to S3.
Deploy the model to an Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference endpoint and submit one request per file.
Deploy the model to an Amazon SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint and invoke it when each file arrives.

correctText: Run an Amazon SageMaker Batch Transform job against the nightly S3 input file and write predictions to S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker offers several inference patterns, and the best choice depends on the shape of the workload. When the input is a file or dataset in Amazon S3 and the goal is to produce predictions for the whole dataset without keeping an endpoint running, Batch Transform is the natural fit. It creates compute for the job, processes the input data, writes output to S3, and avoids a persistent hosting fleet.

Real-time endpoints are optimized for applications that need low-latency responses to individual requests, such as a user-facing API. Serverless Inference reduces infrastructure management for intermittent endpoint traffic, but it is still an endpoint invocation model. Asynchronous Inference queues requests and is useful when requests have large payloads or long processing times but still need near-real-time handling. The mental model is simple: choose an endpoint when an application calls the model, and choose Batch Transform when a dataset is waiting to be scored offline.

For more information, see Deploy models for inference and Use Batch Transform.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A pharmaceutical clinical trials analytics team hosts an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint that predicts whether trial participants will miss their next visit. The team expects future cohorts from new sites to have different enrollment characteristics. The team needs scheduled monitoring that compares live inference traffic with a training baseline and sends alerts when shifts could change how features contribute to predictions. The team wants to avoid writing custom drift detection code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A pharmaceutical clinical trials analytics team hosts an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint that predicts whether trial participants will miss their next visit. The team expects future cohorts from new sites to have different enrollment characteristics. The team needs scheduled monitoring that compares live inference traffic with a training baseline and sends alerts when shifts could change how features contribute to predictions. The team wants to avoid writing custom drift detection code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch dashboard for endpoint invocation count, latency, CPU utilization, and memory utilization metrics.
Create a SageMaker Experiments trial and compare each future model version against the original training job metrics.
Enable endpoint data capture and configure a SageMaker Clarify feature attribution drift monitoring schedule with CloudWatch alarms.
Enable AWS CloudTrail Insights and configure an EventBridge rule to notify the team when endpoint API activity changes.
