correctText: Enable endpoint data capture and configure a SageMaker Clarify feature attribution drift monitoring schedule with CloudWatch alarms.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Model Monitor is designed for monitoring deployed models by running scheduled monitoring jobs, storing monitoring data in Amazon S3, and emitting metrics to CloudWatch. For data distribution concerns, it can compare production traffic to a baseline that represents the expected statistical behavior of training or reference data.

When the concern is that changing live data could alter which features are driving predictions, SageMaker Clarify feature attribution drift is the most direct managed capability. It focuses on changes in feature attribution between the baseline and live data, which is different from only watching endpoint latency or CPU usage. See Monitor feature attribution drift with SageMaker Clarify and Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.

Operational monitoring tools still matter, but they answer different questions. CloudWatch helps you understand whether the endpoint is healthy and responsive, while CloudTrail and CloudTrail Insights help audit or detect unusual AWS API activity. Neither service evaluates whether the model is seeing a shifted population of input data. For data quality drift, SageMaker Model Monitor can also use baseline statistics and constraints, as described in Monitor data quality.

questions.promptHtml: An oceanography institute's ML team is building a SageMaker training environment for models that predict harmful algal blooms. Raw buoy telemetry, satellite images, and vessel observations arrive in multiple formats and must be retained in their native form for future analytics and ML use cases that are not fully known yet. For monthly training jobs, the team repeatedly reads a curated subset that is already staged in object storage and needs very high throughput with low-latency file access. The training jobs can run in a VPC in a single Availability Zone. Which TWO storage choices best meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An oceanography institute's ML team is building a SageMaker training environment for models that predict harmful algal blooms. Raw buoy telemetry, satellite images, and vessel observations arrive in multiple formats and must be retained in their native form for future analytics and ML use cases that are not fully known yet. For monthly training jobs, the team repeatedly reads a curated subset that is already staged in object storage and needs very high throughput with low-latency file access. The training jobs can run in a VPC in a single Availability Zone.

Which TWO storage choices best meet these requirements?

options.text: Store the raw landing data on Amazon EBS volumes attached to a shared notebook instance.
Use Amazon FSx for Lustre with the curated data in Amazon S3 for high-throughput training.
Store the raw landing data in Amazon S3 as a data lake for flexible future processing.
Use Amazon EFS as the primary training store for the curated data already staged in Amazon S3.
Move the curated training subset to an archival Amazon S3 storage class before each training run.

correctText: Use Amazon FSx for Lustre with the curated data in Amazon S3 for high-throughput training.
Store the raw landing data in Amazon S3 as a data lake for flexible future processing.
questions.explanationHtml:
A useful mental model is to separate long-term data retention from active training access. Amazon S3 is commonly used as a data lake because it stores raw data in place, supports many formats, and allows later tools such as Athena, Glue, EMR, and SageMaker workflows to interpret or transform the data when the use case becomes clear. This fits the requirement to retain mixed telemetry, image, and observation data in native form for future ML and analytics.

For the monthly training workload, the requirement changes from flexible storage to high-performance file access. Amazon FSx for Lustre is built for ML and HPC workloads that need high throughput and low latency, and the course material highlights its integration with S3, including reading S3 data through the file system and writing computation outputs back to S3. That makes it a better fit than a general shared file system when curated training data is already in S3 and the workload can operate in a VPC and single Availability Zone.

Amazon EBS is block storage for individual compute resources, not a data lake service. Amazon EFS is valuable for elastic shared NFS storage, but the scenario does not say the data is already in EFS, and the performance requirement maps more directly to FSx for Lustre. Archival S3 storage classes can reduce cost for rarely accessed data, but they introduce retrieval-oriented tradeoffs that are inappropriate for active, repeated training reads.

For more detail, see the AWS documentation for Amazon S3 storage classes, SageMaker training data storage options, Amazon FSx for Lustre, Amazon EFS, and Amazon EBS volume types.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A national museum network's ML platform team stores SageMaker training outputs and approved model artifacts for several projects in a shared Amazon S3 bucket. The exhibit recommendation endpoint uses one SageMaker execution role and must load approved artifacts only from s3://museum-ml-artifacts/models/exhibit-recs/prod/. The artifacts are encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key. Security auditors require least privilege for artifact access and decryption. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A national museum network's ML platform team stores SageMaker training outputs and approved model artifacts for several projects in a shared Amazon S3 bucket. The exhibit recommendation endpoint uses one SageMaker execution role and must load approved artifacts only from s3://museum-ml-artifacts/models/exhibit-recs/prod/. The artifacts are encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key. Security auditors require least privilege for artifact access and decryption.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Attach an IAM policy to the SageMaker execution role that allows S3 read access only to the approved artifact prefix.
Grant the SageMaker execution role full S3 access to the shared bucket and review access with CloudTrail.
Store the customer managed KMS key ID in Secrets Manager and allow the execution role to read that secret.
Attach AmazonSageMakerFullAccess to the SageMaker execution role and separate artifacts by project-owned prefixes.
Grant the SageMaker execution role permission to decrypt the artifacts with the customer managed KMS key.

correctText: Attach an IAM policy to the SageMaker execution role that allows S3 read access only to the approved artifact prefix.
Grant the SageMaker execution role permission to decrypt the artifacts with the customer managed KMS key.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker deployments, think of the execution role as the identity that SageMaker uses to retrieve model artifacts, write logs, and access other AWS resources on behalf of the workload. The role should have only the S3 permissions required for the model artifact location, such as read access to arn:aws:s3:::museum-ml-artifacts/models/exhibit-recs/prod/*, instead of broad access to the shared bucket. The SageMaker role model is described in SageMaker AI execution roles, and S3 policy structure is described in Amazon S3 access policy language overview.

Encryption adds a second authorization layer. Reading an encrypted object from S3 is not enough if the caller is not also allowed to use the relevant AWS KMS key, so the SageMaker execution role needs appropriate KMS permissions for the customer managed key. SageMaker encryption considerations are covered in SageMaker AI encryption at rest, and KMS policy conditions are covered in AWS KMS condition keys.

The main tradeoff is operational convenience versus blast radius. Broad policies such as full SageMaker or full S3 access can make early development easier, but production access should be narrowed once the exact services, actions, and artifact paths are known. CloudTrail remains valuable for auditing access, but auditing does not replace preventive controls in IAM, S3 policies, and KMS key policies.

questions.promptHtml: A regional energy retailer's customer analytics team is using tabular CSV customer usage data in Amazon S3 to predict customer churn. The dataset is less than 100 MB. The team has limited ML engineering capacity and wants Amazon SageMaker to train multiple candidate model types and combine them when this improves validation performance. The team wants the solution with the LEAST custom code. Which approach will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A regional energy retailer's customer analytics team is using tabular CSV customer usage data in Amazon S3 to predict customer churn. The dataset is less than 100 MB. The team has limited ML engineering capacity and wants Amazon SageMaker to train multiple candidate model types and combine them when this improves validation performance. The team wants the solution with the LEAST custom code.

Which approach will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use SageMaker Experiments to compare separate training jobs and deploy the run with the best metric.
Train a SageMaker XGBoost model with automatic model tuning and deploy the best tuned training job.
Create a SageMaker Autopilot job in Ensembling mode to train base models and generate the recommended model.
Create a SageMaker Autopilot job in HPO mode to tune supported algorithms and deploy the best trial.

correctText: Create a SageMaker Autopilot job in Ensembling mode to train base models and generate the recommended model.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Autopilot Ensembling mode is the best fit when the goal is to let AWS automate much of the model selection process for tabular data and combine multiple trained models. In this mode, Autopilot trains several base models using the AutoGluon library and combines them with a stacking ensemble method, which can improve performance when different model types capture different patterns in the data.

HPO mode is still useful, but it has a different optimization strategy. It selects relevant algorithms such as Linear Learner, XGBoost, or deep learning, then searches hyperparameter ranges to find a strong trial. That is not the same as intentionally combining several base models into one stacked model.

Boosting, as used by XGBoost, is also an ensemble technique, but it is an ensemble within a specific algorithm family. It builds a strong model from many weaker tree-based learners, which can be powerful for tabular data, but it does not satisfy the stated need for SageMaker to train multiple candidate model types and combine them with the least custom code.

Use SageMaker Experiments when you need tracking, comparison, and reproducibility across training runs. It is not an automated ensembling service, so it would still require the team to design how separate models are combined. For more information, see SageMaker Autopilot model support and validation, SageMaker Autopilot metrics and validation, and SageMaker XGBoost.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A legal technology startup's ML team trained a PyTorch document classification model on GPU instances in Amazon SageMaker. The team must deploy the model to a SageMaker real-time endpoint for steady business-hours traffic. The endpoint must meet a strict latency target, and the team must minimize inference cost. The engineers are unsure whether the production endpoint needs GPU acceleration or whether a CPU instance will be sufficient. They can run benchmarks before deployment. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST guesswork?
questions.promptText:
A legal technology startup's ML team trained a PyTorch document classification model on GPU instances in Amazon SageMaker. The team must deploy the model to a SageMaker real-time endpoint for steady business-hours traffic. The endpoint must meet a strict latency target, and the team must minimize inference cost. The engineers are unsure whether the production endpoint needs GPU acceleration or whether a CPU instance will be sufficient. They can run benchmarks before deployment.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST guesswork?

options.text: Register the model in SageMaker Model Registry and run SageMaker Inference Recommender to benchmark endpoint configurations against latency and cost goals.
Deploy the model to an AWS Trainium based instance for the real-time endpoint and shift production traffic with a canary deployment.
Convert the workload to SageMaker batch transform and select the lowest priced CPU instance that completes the job overnight.
Deploy the model to the same GPU instance family used during training and use automatic scaling after production traffic is observed.

correctText: Register the model in SageMaker Model Registry and run SageMaker Inference Recommender to benchmark endpoint configurations against latency and cost goals.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Inference Recommender is the best fit when the team needs evidence-based instance selection for a model endpoint. It can benchmark endpoint configurations and provide metrics that help compare latency, throughput, and cost, which is exactly the tradeoff the team needs to evaluate before production deployment. See Amazon SageMaker Inference Recommender.

A common anti-pattern is to reuse the training hardware for inference without validating that it is necessary. Training can benefit from GPUs because backpropagation and large matrix operations are compute intensive, but inference might run acceptably on CPU, optimized CPU silicon, GPU, or specialized inference hardware depending on the model and latency target. AWS also notes that instance choice should consider the workload characteristics rather than assuming one accelerator choice fits all stages, as discussed in Train a Model with Amazon SageMaker and Instance Types for Built-in Algorithms.

Deployment mechanisms such as canary releases and automatic scaling are useful after a candidate endpoint configuration exists. They help manage rollout risk or capacity changes, but they do not replace benchmarking when the core question is whether the model should run on CPU, GPU, or another processor family. Batch transform is also the wrong deployment mode when an application requires real-time responses from a persistent endpoint.

questions.promptHtml: A boutique travel marketplace's ML team uses Amazon SageMaker AI automatic model tuning to tune an XGBoost demand forecasting model. A tuning job was manually stopped after completing many training jobs because the team had to pause work for a budget review. The team will continue with the same training dataset and the same algorithm. The team wants the next tuning run to use the completed results from the earlier run to guide the search and avoid starting from scratch. Which action should the ML engineer take?
questions.promptText:
A boutique travel marketplace's ML team uses Amazon SageMaker AI automatic model tuning to tune an XGBoost demand forecasting model. A tuning job was manually stopped after completing many training jobs because the team had to pause work for a budget review. The team will continue with the same training dataset and the same algorithm. The team wants the next tuning run to use the completed results from the earlier run to guide the search and avoid starting from scratch.

Which action should the ML engineer take?

options.text: Configure random search on a new tuning job and run all training jobs in parallel.
Configure early stopping to Auto on a new tuning job and omit parent tuning jobs.
Configure a warm start tuning job with IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM and use the earlier tuning job as the parent.
Configure a warm start tuning job with TRANSFER_LEARNING and use the earlier tuning job as the parent.

correctText: Configure a warm start tuning job with IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM and use the earlier tuning job as the parent.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker AI automatic model tuning runs multiple training jobs with different hyperparameter values and evaluates them against an objective metric. When a tuning effort has useful completed trials, a warm start tuning job can use results from previous tuning jobs as a starting point for the next search rather than treating the next run as completely new.

The important distinction is that warm start works at the tuning-job level. It uses prior completed training-job outcomes to inform which hyperparameter combinations to try next, but it is not the same as resuming a partially completed individual training job from a checkpoint. For the same dataset and same algorithm, IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM is the appropriate warm start type.

Early stopping is a different optimization. It helps reduce wasted training time when an individual training job is not improving the objective metric significantly, but it does not reuse the search history from a prior tuning job. Random search can run trials independently and in parallel, but that independence is exactly why it does not meet the requirement to learn from the previous tuning run.

For more information, see the AWS documentation for Overview of SageMaker AI Automatic Model Tuning and the CreateHyperParameterTuningJob API.

questions.promptHtml: A municipal transit agency's ML team is preparing tabular CSV data in Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to train a binary classification model that predicts whether a bus trip will arrive late. One input column, fare_payment_type, contains one of three values: cash, mobile_app, or transit_card. The values are categories, not ranks. The team wants to transform this column into numeric input while preserving the distinction among the categories for training. Which preprocessing step should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A municipal transit agency's ML team is preparing tabular CSV data in Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to train a binary classification model that predicts whether a bus trip will arrive late. One input column, fare_payment_type, contains one of three values: cash, mobile_app, or transit_card. The values are categories, not ranks. The team wants to transform this column into numeric input while preserving the distinction among the categories for training.

Which preprocessing step should the team use?

options.text: Apply one-hot encoding to create separate indicator features for the fare_payment_type values.
Apply tokenization to split the fare_payment_type values into word tokens before training.
Apply label encoding to replace the fare_payment_type values with sequential integer identifiers.
Apply logarithmic transformation to the fare_payment_type values after converting them to numbers.

correctText: Apply one-hot encoding to create separate indicator features for the fare_payment_type values.
questions.explanationHtml:
One-hot encoding is the usual choice for an unordered categorical feature with a small number of possible values. It creates binary indicator columns, such as fare_payment_type_cash and fare_payment_type_mobile_app, so the model can learn separate effects for each category without assuming that one payment type is greater than another.

Label encoding can be useful in some contexts, especially when the category values have a real ordinal meaning or when an algorithm is designed to handle encoded categories appropriately. In this scenario, the values are names of payment methods, so assigning values such as 0, 1, and 2 can accidentally introduce an ordering or spacing that does not exist in the data.

Tokenization is a different encoding step that is common for text features. For example, a document classification workflow might tokenize article text before converting tokens into numeric vectors, but a three-value tabular category is better handled as a categorical feature. Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler includes built-in transformations for preparing ML data, including categorical encoding workflows, as described in Transform Data.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A health insurance actuarial team is moving a scikit-learn risk scoring model into Amazon SageMaker. The team already has Python training and inference scripts that use common Python libraries. The team does not need custom operating system packages or a specialized model server. The team wants to minimize container maintenance while still using its own model code. Which container approach should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A health insurance actuarial team is moving a scikit-learn risk scoring model into Amazon SageMaker. The team already has Python training and inference scripts that use common Python libraries. The team does not need custom operating system packages or a specialized model server. The team wants to minimize container maintenance while still using its own model code.

Which container approach should the team use?

options.text: Use a SageMaker-provided scikit-learn framework container and supply the custom Python scripts.
Build a custom Docker image from a base Linux image and push the image to Amazon ECR.
Package the model code as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate and run inference there.
Use SageMaker Training Compiler with a custom Docker image and configure the estimator.

correctText: Use a SageMaker-provided scikit-learn framework container and supply the custom Python scripts.
questions.explanationHtml:
When model code uses a common framework such as scikit-learn and does not require custom operating system packages or a custom serving stack, the lowest-maintenance choice is usually a SageMaker-provided framework container. SageMaker supplies containers for common ML frameworks, and the ML engineer can provide the Python entry point and model code while SageMaker handles the training and hosting integration around the container.

Custom containers are still important, but they are best reserved for cases where the managed images do not fit, for example an unsupported framework, unusual dependencies, or a specialized inference server. Building from a base image and pushing to Amazon ECR gives maximum flexibility, but it also shifts patching, dependency management, and container contract responsibilities to the team.

Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate is a general-purpose serverless container option, but it is not the least-effort path for a standard SageMaker training and inference workflow. SageMaker Training Compiler is also the wrong fit because it addresses a training optimization problem for supported deep learning workloads rather than the container selection problem described here.

For more detail, see SageMaker container decision guidance and SageMaker pre-built Docker containers.

questions.promptHtml: An agricultural cooperative's crop insurance analytics team trains a tabular Amazon SageMaker model to predict claim risk. Before deployment, underwriters require a report that identifies whether the training data or model behavior shows potential bias across applicant groups and which input columns have the largest influence on predictions. Which action should the ML engineer take?
questions.promptText:
An agricultural cooperative's crop insurance analytics team trains a tabular Amazon SageMaker model to predict claim risk. Before deployment, underwriters require a report that identifies whether the training data or model behavior shows potential bias across applicant groups and which input columns have the largest influence on predictions.

Which action should the ML engineer take?

options.text: Run a SageMaker Clarify analysis job to calculate bias metrics and SHAP feature attributions.
Run SageMaker Experiments tracking to compare validation metrics across training runs and trials.
Run a SageMaker Model Monitor schedule to create data quality and model quality baselines.
Run CloudWatch Logs Insights queries to aggregate prediction logs and count errors by group.

correctText: Run a SageMaker Clarify analysis job to calculate bias metrics and SHAP feature attributions.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Clarify is the SageMaker capability used when an ML engineer needs insight into both potential bias and model explainability. Clarify can analyze training data for pre-training bias, analyze model predictions for post-training bias, and generate feature attributions that explain how input features contribute to predictions.

For explainability, Clarify uses Shapley value concepts through SHAP approximations. The practical mental model is that Clarify asks how predictions change when features are included or excluded, then assigns contribution values to features so teams can understand which inputs are driving model behavior.

This differs from SageMaker Model Monitor, which is mainly a production monitoring service for detecting data quality drift, model quality drift, bias drift, and feature attribution drift after a model is deployed. CloudWatch Logs Insights and SageMaker Experiments are useful operational and experiment-tracking tools, but they do not replace Clarify's bias and explainability analyses.

For more information, see Measure Pretraining Bias, Measure Posttraining Bias, and Shapley Values for Explainability.

questions.promptHtml: An aerospace parts manufacturer's ML team uses Amazon SageMaker AI automatic model tuning for a PyTorch defect classification model. A tuning job was stopped after completing many training jobs because a budget alarm fired. The team has increased the budget and wants the next tuning job to use the same training data and algorithm. The next job must use the completed trials to guide which hyperparameter combinations to evaluate next. Which action will meet these requirements with the LEAST wasted work?
questions.promptText:
An aerospace parts manufacturer's ML team uses Amazon SageMaker AI automatic model tuning for a PyTorch defect classification model. A tuning job was stopped after completing many training jobs because a budget alarm fired. The team has increased the budget and wants the next tuning job to use the same training data and algorithm. The next job must use the completed trials to guide which hyperparameter combinations to evaluate next.

Which action will meet these requirements with the LEAST wasted work?

options.text: Enable early stopping set to Auto and rerun the tuning job without referencing the prior tuning job.
Create a warm start tuning job with IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM and specify the stopped tuning job as the parent.
Restore the latest training checkpoint and continue only the best completed training job outside automatic tuning.
Create a new tuning job with the same hyperparameter ranges and increase the maximum number of parallel training jobs.

correctText: Create a warm start tuning job with IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM and specify the stopped tuning job as the parent.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker AI automatic model tuning runs multiple training jobs with different hyperparameter values and uses an objective metric to identify the best model. When a tuning effort has already produced useful trial results, a warm start tuning job is the right mechanism to reuse that search history instead of beginning from scratch.

The IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM warm start type fits a follow-up tuning job that uses the same dataset and algorithm. This allows the tuner to use prior observations to guide the next combinations to evaluate, which is different from simply launching another tuning job with the same ranges.

Early stopping is a useful cost-control feature, especially for algorithms that emit objective metrics during training, but it solves a different problem. It helps stop unpromising training jobs inside a tuning job, while warm start helps a later tuning job benefit from previous tuning work.

Increasing parallel training jobs can shorten wall-clock duration, but it can reduce the opportunity for sequential learning from previous trials and can increase spend. For an interrupted tuning effort, the practical refinement pattern is to preserve the information already learned, then continue the search using the correct warm start mode. For more information, see Automatic model tuning and How hyperparameter tuning works.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A digital advertising exchange's ML operations team is reviewing Amazon SageMaker endpoint instance choices during a quarterly right-sizing effort. CloudWatch metrics show one real-time endpoint for a scikit-learn feature scoring service is consistently CPU-bound while memory utilization remains low. A second endpoint runs a deep learning ranking model and needs higher inference throughput at lower cost. The team wants to choose instance families based on workload characteristics before validating performance with load tests. Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A digital advertising exchange's ML operations team is reviewing Amazon SageMaker endpoint instance choices during a quarterly right-sizing effort. CloudWatch metrics show one real-time endpoint for a scikit-learn feature scoring service is consistently CPU-bound while memory utilization remains low. A second endpoint runs a deep learning ranking model and needs higher inference throughput at lower cost. The team wants to choose instance families based on workload characteristics before validating performance with load tests.

Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move the deep learning inference endpoint to an AWS Inferentia powered instance family and compare throughput and cost.
Move the CPU-bound endpoint variant to a memory optimized instance family and keep the current request pattern.
Move both endpoint variants to a larger general purpose instance family and scale for peak traffic manually.
Move the CPU-bound endpoint variant to a compute optimized instance family and validate latency under expected traffic.
Move the deep learning inference endpoint to an AWS Trainium powered instance family and compare training duration.

correctText: Move the deep learning inference endpoint to an AWS Inferentia powered instance family and compare throughput and cost.
Move the CPU-bound endpoint variant to a compute optimized instance family and validate latency under expected traffic.
questions.explanationHtml:
Instance families are designed around different hardware tradeoffs. A compute optimized family is a better fit for CPU-bound inference when memory is not the limiting resource, while a memory optimized family is better suited to workloads that need more memory capacity or memory bandwidth.

For deep learning inference, AWS Inferentia powered instances are designed to improve inference throughput and cost efficiency. A Trainium based endpoint choice would still need to be judged with inference metrics for the deployed model, so comparing training duration does not satisfy the stated objective.

The right mental model is to match the dominant bottleneck first, then validate with measured traffic. Amazon SageMaker Inference Recommender can automate load tests across endpoint configurations and report metrics such as cost, latency, and throughput, but it does not remove the need to understand whether the workload is CPU-bound, memory-bound, or suited to specialized ML inference hardware. For more background, see Amazon EC2 instance types, SageMaker AI instance types, and Amazon SageMaker Inference Recommender.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A subscription video platform's ML operations team maintains a containerized feature scoring service on Amazon ECS. The team has separate staging and production ECS services. When code is committed, the team wants to run unit tests, build the container image, package the deployment artifact, deploy to staging, run integration tests, wait for a manual approval, and then deploy the same artifact to production. The team wants managed orchestration with clear stage visibility and minimal custom scripting. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A subscription video platform's ML operations team maintains a containerized feature scoring service on Amazon ECS. The team has separate staging and production ECS services. When code is committed, the team wants to run unit tests, build the container image, package the deployment artifact, deploy to staging, run integration tests, wait for a manual approval, and then deploy the same artifact to production. The team wants managed orchestration with clear stage visibility and minimal custom scripting.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a CodeDeploy deployment group that pulls source code, builds the container image, runs tests, and deploys the image to both ECS services by using lifecycle hooks.
Create a CodeBuild project that pulls the repository, runs tests, builds the image, updates both ECS services from the buildspec, and pauses by waiting for an operator input file in Amazon S3.

Create a CodePipeline with Source, Build, DeployToStaging, IntegrationTest, Approval, and DeployToProduction stages. Use CodeBuild for tests and image packaging, and use separate CodeDeploy deployment groups for the two ECS services.
Create EventBridge rules that start separate CodeBuild projects for testing and packaging and start separate CodePipeline executions for staging and production on each source change.

correctText: Create a CodePipeline with Source, Build, DeployToStaging, IntegrationTest, Approval, and DeployToProduction stages. Use CodeBuild for tests and image packaging, and use separate CodeDeploy deployment groups for the two ECS services.
questions.explanationHtml:
CodePipeline is the managed orchestration service for CI/CD workflows on AWS. A pipeline is composed of stages and actions, such as source, build, test, approval, and deploy, and artifacts flow between those actions. This model fits a release process that must deploy to staging, run an integration test action against staging, and require approval before production. See CodePipeline concepts for the core model of pipelines, stages, actions, transitions, and artifacts.

CodeBuild fits the build and test responsibilities in this scenario. A build action can run commands from a buildspec.yml, execute unit tests, build a container image, and produce the deployable artifact, while a later CodeBuild action can run integration tests after the staging deployment. The CodeBuild action reference for CodePipeline and the CodeBuild buildspec reference describe how CodeBuild participates in pipelines and how build phases and artifacts are defined.

CodeDeploy is used for the deployment responsibility, not for compiling or packaging the application. Separate deployment groups are a clean way to represent separate environments such as staging and production, and CodePipeline can pass the same artifact through staging validation before allowing the production deployment. The CodeDeploy deployment groups documentation explains how deployment groups define target resources and environment-specific deployment behavior.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: An online education provider's ML operations team runs a student dropout prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The endpoint has data capture enabled, and the team has baseline quality constraints from validation data. The team wants to initiate a retraining workflow when production monitoring shows sustained degradation, then track the retrained model as a new version for approval before deployment. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST custom orchestration?
questions.promptText:
An online education provider's ML operations team runs a student dropout prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The endpoint has data capture enabled, and the team has baseline quality constraints from validation data. The team wants to initiate a retraining workflow when production monitoring shows sustained degradation, then track the retrained model as a new version for approval before deployment.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST custom orchestration?

options.text: Configure an EventBridge scheduled rule to run SageMaker batch transform on captured endpoint data and update the endpoint with the generated output artifact.
Configure SageMaker Model Monitor on the endpoint, use CloudWatch and EventBridge to start a SageMaker Pipeline that retrains the model and registers the model package.
Configure SageMaker Experiments to compare production predictions, start a training job from the best trial, and overwrite the existing endpoint configuration.
Configure QuickSight anomaly detection on captured prediction data, publish a dashboard, and manually launch a SageMaker training job when anomalies appear.

correctText: Configure SageMaker Model Monitor on the endpoint, use CloudWatch and EventBridge to start a SageMaker Pipeline that retrains the model and registers the model package.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Model Monitor is designed for the production side of the ML lifecycle: it compares observed inference data and predictions against a baseline so teams can detect data drift, quality drift, bias, or explainability changes. When degradation crosses an operational threshold, the usual pattern is to connect monitoring output to automation rather than retrain on a fixed schedule or rely on someone watching a dashboard.

SageMaker Pipelines is the managed workflow service for defining repeatable ML steps such as processing captured data, training, evaluating, and registering the resulting model. EventBridge can be used to start a pipeline execution, and the SageMaker Model Registry provides versioned model packages so a retrained model can be reviewed and approved before deployment. This gives the team a traceable retraining mechanism without building a custom orchestration system from scratch.

Batch transform is a poor fit because it generates predictions for a dataset rather than producing a new trained model. SageMaker Experiments is valuable for experiment tracking, but it is not the production degradation detector. QuickSight can support analysis and dashboards, but using it as the retraining trigger creates a manual operational loop rather than an automated MLOps workflow.

For more information, see Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor overview, Scheduling or event-triggering SageMaker Pipeline runs with Amazon EventBridge, SageMaker Pipelines step types, and SageMaker Model Registry concepts.

Use Amazon MWAA with a managed Airflow DAG to run CodeBuild, SageMaker training, model registration, and endpoint deployment tasks.

correctText: Use SageMaker Projects with a built-in MLOps template to create CodePipeline, CodeBuild, SageMaker Pipelines, and Model Registry workflows.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Projects is designed for SageMaker-native MLOps workflows that connect source control, automated builds, ML workflow execution, model registration, and deployment automation. In this scenario, the team needs more than an ML workflow graph, it needs a repeatable CI/CD release path from code change through approved production deployment.

A good mental model is that SageMaker Pipelines orchestrates the ML steps, such as processing, training, evaluation, and registration, while CodePipeline orchestrates the software release flow, such as source, build, deploy, and approval stages. Model Registry provides version tracking and approval state for model packages, which supports traceability and controlled promotion.

Amazon MWAA and EventBridge are valid orchestration services, but they are not the lowest-overhead choice for this SageMaker CI/CD requirement. They would require more custom glue logic to reproduce the build, train, approve, and deploy pattern that SageMaker Projects templates are intended to accelerate.

The team wants to start from a pre-trained foundation model and avoid building custom training containers or training a model from random weights. questions.promptText:
A regional energy utility's customer operations team wants to adapt a generative AI model to produce outage notification responses in the utility's approved style. The team has a curated supervised dataset of prompts and desired responses stored in Amazon S3. The team wants to start from a pre-trained foundation model and avoid building custom training containers or training a model from random weights.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Use SageMaker JumpStart to fine-tune a supported foundation model with the Amazon S3 training dataset.
Use Amazon Comprehend custom classification to train a text category prediction model.
Use SageMaker Training to train a new PyTorch transformer model from random initialization.
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to retrieve company documents at inference time.

correctText: Use SageMaker JumpStart to fine-tune a supported foundation model with the Amazon S3 training dataset.
questions.explanationHtml:
Fine-tuning is the right fit when a team has supervised examples that show how a model should respond for a task or style. In this scenario, the team is not merely asking the model to reference company documents, it wants to adapt a pre-trained foundation model by training on curated prompt and response examples stored in Amazon S3.

SageMaker JumpStart provides a managed path for using pre-trained foundation models and fine-tuning supported models with a custom dataset, which avoids the operational work of creating a training container from scratch. The workflow is aligned with the practical model development guidance to reuse pre-trained models when possible instead of spending unnecessary compute and engineering effort on training a large model from random weights. For details, see SageMaker JumpStart fine-tuning workflow in Studio and SageMaker JumpStart foundation model fine-tuning reference.

Amazon Bedrock also supports model customization for supported foundation models, and its documentation describes fine-tuning with prepared datasets in Amazon S3, as shown in Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning overview and Amazon Bedrock dataset preparation requirements. However, a retrieval approach such as a knowledge base is a different pattern: it supplies context at inference time rather than updating a model through supervised fine-tuning. Training a new model from scratch or using a classification-specific service would add effort or solve the wrong problem.

questions.promptHtml: A legal aid nonprofit's data science team is preparing a text classification training dataset from raw intake forms and call transcripts stored in Amazon S3. The forms and transcripts are in English and can contain names, addresses, phone numbers, and case details. Compliance requires the team to identify sensitive data in the S3 data lake, remove or mask PII before model training, and avoid writing custom detection code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A legal aid nonprofit's data science team is preparing a text classification training dataset from raw intake forms and call transcripts stored in Amazon S3. The forms and transcripts are in English and can contain names, addresses, phone numbers, and case details. Compliance requires the team to identify sensitive data in the S3 data lake, remove or mask PII before model training, and avoid writing custom detection code.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Athena to drop known PII columns from S3 queries, and train only from the resulting query output files in S3.
Use S3 Object Lambda to redact analyst downloads from S3, and train the model from the original object locations in S3.
Use SageMaker notebooks with broad S3 read access, and require analysts to manually delete PII before each training run.
Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in S3, and run Amazon Comprehend PII redaction before writing curated training files to S3.

correctText: Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in S3, and run Amazon Comprehend PII redaction before writing curated training files to S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
For compliance-sensitive ML data preparation, the safer pattern is to keep raw data separate from an approved, curated training dataset. Amazon Macie is designed to discover sensitive data in Amazon S3, including categories such as PII, which helps teams understand where regulated data exists before it enters the ML workflow. For text data in a supported language, Amazon Comprehend can detect and redact PII, so the training files written back to S3 contain masked or removed sensitive values instead of the original raw content.

Athena is useful for querying S3 data and removing known columns, but PII in intake forms and transcripts can appear inside free text, not only in predictable columns. S3 Object Lambda can be useful for transforming objects at retrieval time, but it must be used through the configured access path and does not automatically create a persistent curated training dataset. Manual notebook-based cleanup is an operational anti-pattern for compliance because it is hard to audit, hard to reproduce, and likely to violate least privilege. For more information, see Amazon Macie managed data identifiers and Amazon Comprehend PII detection and redaction.

questions.promptHtml: A private wealth management firm's ML platform team uses Amazon SageMaker Studio to develop models and SageMaker training jobs to train on sensitive portfolio data in Amazon S3. The security team requires the Studio environment and training jobs to avoid public internet paths when accessing AWS services. The notebooks and training jobs must still read and write S3 data. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A private wealth management firm's ML platform team uses Amazon SageMaker Studio to develop models and SageMaker training jobs to train on sensitive portfolio data in Amazon S3. The security team requires the Studio environment and training jobs to avoid public internet paths when accessing AWS services. The notebooks and training jobs must still read and write S3 data.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Place Studio apps and training jobs in public subnets. Attach security groups that block inbound access. Use an internet gateway for S3 and API calls.
Create the SageMaker Studio domain with default internet access. Run training jobs in default VPC subnets. Restrict S3 data with KMS keys and IAM policies.
Enable SageMaker network isolation for every training job. Use the default SageMaker managed network. Allow S3 access through the container execution role.
Create the SageMaker Studio domain in VPC-only mode. Run training jobs in private VPC subnets with security groups. Add VPC endpoints for S3 and SageMaker access.

correctText: Create the SageMaker Studio domain in VPC-only mode. Run training jobs in private VPC subnets with security groups. Add VPC endpoints for S3 and SageMaker access.
questions.explanationHtml:
For sensitive ML workloads, a common network control is to place SageMaker resources into a customer VPC and use VPC endpoints so AWS service traffic does not need to traverse public internet paths. In SageMaker Studio, choosing a restricted network mode such as VpcOnly shifts responsibility to the VPC design, including private subnets, security groups, and endpoints for required services. See SageMaker Studio network access modes for how Studio network access is controlled.

Training jobs that need VPC access are configured with VPC subnets and security groups, and they commonly need an S3 VPC endpoint so training data and model artifacts can move to and from Amazon S3 without requiring internet routing. The relevant SageMaker training configuration pattern is described in Give SageMaker training jobs access to resources in your Amazon VPC. For private access to SageMaker APIs or runtime endpoints from within a VPC, interface endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink are described in Connect to SageMaker through an interface VPC endpoint.

It is important to separate network path controls from other security controls. IAM and KMS help with authorization and encryption, but they do not by themselves determine whether traffic uses an internet gateway. SageMaker network isolation is also a different control: it restricts container network access, which can be useful for untrusted code, but it does not replace the VPC endpoint design needed for private access to AWS services.

questions.promptHtml: A cruise line's revenue management team is preparing tabular booking, cabin, and loyalty data for a demand forecasting model. The raw data is in Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. The team wants to explore and transform the data visually, then make the resulting features reusable for future training jobs and available to applications that need current feature values for inference. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A cruise line's revenue management team is preparing tabular booking, cabin, and loyalty data for a demand forecasting model. The raw data is in Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. The team wants to explore and transform the data visually, then make the resulting features reusable for future training jobs and available to applications that need current feature values for inference.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Load the data into Amazon QuickSight, create calculated fields, and publish the dashboard dataset for training and inference.
Import the data into SageMaker Data Wrangler, build the transformations, and export the prepared features to SageMaker Feature Store.
Query the data with Amazon Athena, write transformed Parquet files to Amazon S3, and have inference applications read the files directly.
Create AWS Glue DataBrew recipes for the transformations, write the output to Amazon S3, and version the files with S3 object versioning.

correctText: Import the data into SageMaker Data Wrangler, build the transformations, and export the prepared features to SageMaker Feature Store.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Data Wrangler is designed for interactive ML data preparation. It can import from sources such as Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift, let engineers visualize and transform data, and then export the resulting flow or prepared data for downstream ML workflows. See the AWS documentation for Data Wrangler overview and Data Wrangler import.

SageMaker Feature Store is the managed repository for organizing and sharing features across models and teams. Its online store supports low-latency access patterns for current feature values, while its offline store supports batch access for training and analysis. Data Wrangler can export prepared features into Feature Store, which avoids building a separate ingestion and cataloging mechanism for transformed ML features. See Data Wrangler export and SageMaker Feature Store.

Athena, Glue DataBrew, and QuickSight can each play useful roles in data analysis or preparation, but they do not by themselves provide a managed feature repository with online and offline feature access. For this scenario, the important tradeoff is not only preparing the data, but also publishing the prepared features in a way that improves consistency and reuse across training and inference.

questions.promptHtml: An automotive safety testing lab's ML platform team uses Amazon SageMaker Studio notebooks and SageMaker training jobs with crash sensor data in Amazon S3. Security policy requires the notebooks and training containers to avoid direct internet access. The training jobs must still access S3 data and SageMaker services from inside the VPC. Which solution should the team implement?
questions.promptText:
An automotive safety testing lab's ML platform team uses Amazon SageMaker Studio notebooks and SageMaker training jobs with crash sensor data in Amazon S3. Security policy requires the notebooks and training containers to avoid direct internet access. The training jobs must still access S3 data and SageMaker services from inside the VPC.

Which solution should the team implement?

options.text: Keep Studio internet access enabled in public subnets, require TLS and SSE-KMS on S3, create an S3 endpoint, and scope IAM policies to required data paths.

Configure Studio for VPC Only in private subnets, run training jobs in the VPC, add required VPC endpoints including S3 and SageMaker service endpoints, and scope IAM and bucket policies to required data paths.
Embed access keys in notebook code, route traffic through an internet gateway, require TLS for service calls, and encrypt training outputs with a KMS key.
Enable network isolation for all training jobs, remove private service endpoints from the VPC, rely on the SageMaker service role, and allow S3 access through public service endpoints.

correctText: Configure Studio for VPC Only in private subnets, run training jobs in the VPC, add required VPC endpoints including S3 and SageMaker service endpoints, and scope IAM and bucket policies to required data paths.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a private SageMaker environment, the mental model is that network reachability, identity authorization, and data protection are separate controls. VPC Only mode and private subnets reduce internet exposure, VPC endpoints provide private connectivity to AWS services, and IAM plus S3 bucket policies define who can access which resources. For Studio notebooks and training jobs that must stay private, the design should include the required private paths for S3 data access and SageMaker service access, with additional supporting endpoints added only when the workflow needs those service calls.

Encryption controls such as TLS and KMS are important, but they do not by themselves make a workload private or least privilege. Similarly, network isolation can reduce container communication, but it must be planned together with required service access because SageMaker workloads commonly need to retrieve data, use authorized roles, write artifacts, and emit operational data. Private connectivity for SageMaker APIs and runtime is covered in Connect to SageMaker AI through an interface VPC endpoint, while SageMaker security and IAM controls are covered in SageMaker AI security overview and Identity and access management for SageMaker AI.

questions.promptHtml: A national museum's digital collections team is training an image metadata classifier in Amazon SageMaker. The team is comparing several candidate models before deployment and wants to identify whether a candidate has learned too little structure from the data or has learned patterns that do not generalize. The team has labeled data available for both training and evaluation. Which approach should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A national museum's digital collections team is training an image metadata classifier in Amazon SageMaker. The team is comparing several candidate models before deployment and wants to identify whether a candidate has learned too little structure from the data or has learned patterns that do not generalize. The team has labeled data available for both training and evaluation.

Which approach should the team use?

options.text: Rank each candidate by its final training accuracy and select the model with the highest training score.
Plot training and validation metrics for each candidate and compare the gap between the curves across epochs.
Deploy each candidate to an endpoint and compare invocation latency before reviewing evaluation metrics.
Increase the number of epochs for each candidate and compare only the last training loss value.

correctText: Plot training and validation metrics for each candidate and compare the gap between the curves across epochs.
questions.explanationHtml:
To identify underfitting and overfitting, compare model behavior on data used for training with behavior on labeled data that was held out for evaluation. If both training and validation performance are poor, the model may be too simple, insufficiently trained, or missing important features. If training performance keeps improving while validation performance stalls or worsens, the model is likely learning artifacts of the training data instead of generalizable patterns.

In SageMaker model development, plotting training and validation curves is a practical way to see these patterns across epochs rather than relying on a single final metric. This also informs the next action, such as using regularization, early stopping, more representative data, or a simpler model when validation performance diverges from training performance. AWS discusses these concepts in Model fit: underfitting vs. overfitting, model evaluation with held-out data in Evaluating ML models, and SageMaker training and validation curve analysis in Plot training and validation curves.

questions.promptHtml: A pharmaceutical manufacturing quality team is preparing sensor and lab-result datasets for ML experiments. The team has an existing NAS-based workflow that is used by Linux and Windows applications. Analysts frequently create isolated point-in-time copies of the file system to test preprocessing changes without duplicating all the underlying data. The team wants a managed AWS storage service that requires the fewest workflow changes. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A pharmaceutical manufacturing quality team is preparing sensor and lab-result datasets for ML experiments. The team has an existing NAS-based workflow that is used by Linux and Windows applications. Analysts frequently create isolated point-in-time copies of the file system to test preprocessing changes without duplicating all the underlying data. The team wants a managed AWS storage service that requires the fewest workflow changes.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP as the shared file system for the preprocessing workflow.
Use Amazon S3 as the central data store and update the applications to access objects directly.
Use Amazon EFS as the shared file system for all preprocessing clients by using NFS.
Use Amazon EBS volumes attached to a shared Amazon EC2 preprocessing instance.

correctText: Use Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP as the shared file system for the preprocessing workflow.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is designed for managed ONTAP file storage on AWS, which makes it a good fit when an existing workflow depends on NAS-style access rather than object access. It supports shared access from multiple client types and protocols, including NFS and SMB, which aligns with mixed Linux and Windows preprocessing environments. The ONTAP capabilities, such as snapshots, storage efficiency, and cloning, help teams test data preparation changes without creating full physical copies each time. See the AWS documentation for What is Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP? and Accessing data from within AWS.

Amazon S3 is often the right foundation for ML data lakes because it stores objects at large scale and integrates with analytics and ML services, but it is not a drop-in replacement for applications that expect a mounted file system. Amazon EFS provides elastic shared file storage through NFS and is useful for many Linux-oriented shared file workloads, but it is not the best match for preserving a mixed-protocol ONTAP NAS workflow. Amazon EBS is block storage attached to EC2 instances, so using it as a shared preprocessing hub would add operational bottlenecks instead of providing a managed shared file data source. For comparison, see the AWS overviews for Amazon S3 and Amazon EFS.

questions.promptHtml: A municipal water authority's reliability analytics team has CSV files in Amazon S3 with labeled maintenance history, sensor summary fields, and a target column that indicates whether a pump failed within 30 days. The team wants to quickly choose a baseline modeling approach for this binary classification problem. The team has limited experience selecting algorithms and tuning hyperparameters, but wants to inspect the candidate models before deciding what to deploy. Which modeling approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST manual effort?
questions.promptText:
A municipal water authority's reliability analytics team has CSV files in Amazon S3 with labeled maintenance history, sensor summary fields, and a target column that indicates whether a pump failed within 30 days. The team wants to quickly choose a baseline modeling approach for this binary classification problem. The team has limited experience selecting algorithms and tuning hyperparameters, but wants to inspect the candidate models before deciding what to deploy.

Which modeling approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST manual effort?

options.text: Use SageMaker JumpStart to fine-tune a pretrained foundation model on the maintenance records.
Use Amazon SageMaker Autopilot to create an AutoML job and review the generated model candidates.
Use the SageMaker built-in k-means algorithm to cluster pumps and assign failure labels afterward.
Use the SageMaker built-in XGBoost algorithm and manually tune the primary hyperparameters.

correctText: Use Amazon SageMaker Autopilot to create an AutoML job and review the generated model candidates.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Autopilot is designed for situations where the team has tabular data and wants automated help with choosing a model, preprocessing data, training candidates, tuning hyperparameters, and comparing results. For a labeled binary classification problem, this is a strong fit because it can generate candidate models and rank them, while still giving engineers a way to inspect what was produced rather than treating the process as a complete black box.

Choosing a single built-in algorithm such as XGBoost can be effective, but it shifts more responsibility to the engineer to decide that XGBoost is the right starting point and to tune its hyperparameters. K-means is the wrong modeling family because it is unsupervised and does not directly optimize against the target label. Fine-tuning a foundation model through JumpStart is also an overcomplicated modeling choice for structured CSV data when the problem is conventional tabular classification.

The practical mental model is to start with the simplest service that matches the data shape, label availability, and required control. Autopilot is useful when the team needs a fast, inspectable baseline for tabular classification or regression, while built-in algorithms and custom containers are better when the team already knows the modeling approach or needs more implementation control. For more information, see Automate model development with Amazon SageMaker Autopilot, SageMaker Autopilot model support and validation, and Choose an algorithm.

questions.promptHtml: A specialty insurance underwriter's data science team is training a tabular claim severity model in Amazon SageMaker. The latest experiment has much lower error on the training set than on the validation set. The dataset has hundreds of engineered features, many of which are weakly predictive or correlated with other features. The team wants to improve generalization without increasing model complexity. Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A specialty insurance underwriter's data science team is training a tabular claim severity model in Amazon SageMaker. The latest experiment has much lower error on the training set than on the validation set. The dataset has hundreds of engineered features, many of which are weakly predictive or correlated with other features. The team wants to improve generalization without increasing model complexity.

Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Remove low-value or redundant features before the next training run.
Add all available raw features and rely on more epochs to learn relevance.
Run a grid search across every hyperparameter with maximum parallel jobs.
Increase model depth and continue training until training loss stops decreasing.
Increase L1 or L2 regularization while evaluating results on validation data.

correctText: Remove low-value or redundant features before the next training run.
Increase L1 or L2 regularization while evaluating results on validation data.
questions.explanationHtml:
A model that performs much better on training data than on validation data is showing a classic sign of overfitting. The model has learned patterns in the training set that do not generalize well, so the response should reduce unnecessary complexity, add constraints, or improve validation discipline rather than optimize only for training loss.

Regularization is a standard way to constrain a model. In SageMaker Linear Learner, for example, l1 represents L1 regularization and wd represents L2 weight decay, as described in Linear Learner hyperparameters. For tree-based models such as XGBoost, AWS documents several hyperparameters that can affect model complexity and overfitting behavior in XGBoost hyperparameters.

Feature selection is another practical control. Reducing weak, redundant, or highly correlated features helps avoid the curse of dimensionality and can make the model easier to fit and explain. SageMaker Data Wrangler includes analyses related to feature selection and multicollinearity, including PCA, VIF, and Lasso-based feature selection, as described in Analyze and visualize data in Data Wrangler.

Increasing depth, adding every feature, or training until training loss stops improving all push the model toward memorizing the training data. A broad grid search across every hyperparameter is also wasteful and can obscure the real issue. The better mental model is to compare training and validation behavior, then constrain or simplify the model until validation performance improves, as discussed in Analyze training and validation curves.

questions.promptHtml: An online education platform's ML operations team hosts a course recommendation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. During enrollment deadlines, traffic increases sharply, endpoint latency rises, and host utilization metrics are consistently high. The team must keep the model available for interactive requests and wants to reduce manual capacity changes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
An online education platform's ML operations team hosts a course recommendation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. During enrollment deadlines, traffic increases sharply, endpoint latency rises, and host utilization metrics are consistently high. The team must keep the model available for interactive requests and wants to reduce manual capacity changes.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail Insights, and create EventBridge notifications for unusual SageMaker API activity.
Move the workload to SageMaker Batch Transform, and run prediction jobs during expected enrollment deadlines.
Enable SageMaker Model Monitor schedules, and configure alerts for data quality drift against a baseline dataset.
Monitor endpoint latency and utilization in Amazon CloudWatch, and configure SageMaker endpoint auto scaling for the production variant.

correctText: Monitor endpoint latency and utilization in Amazon CloudWatch, and configure SageMaker endpoint auto scaling for the production variant.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon CloudWatch is the operational monitoring service to use when a deployed SageMaker endpoint has latency or utilization issues. SageMaker emits endpoint metrics such as invocations, latency, errors, and host utilization to CloudWatch, which lets an ML operations team confirm whether performance degradation aligns with traffic or resource pressure. See Monitor Amazon SageMaker AI with Amazon CloudWatch.

After the team confirms that load is driving latency, SageMaker endpoint auto scaling is the managed way to adjust provisioned capacity for a real-time endpoint. Instead of manually changing instance counts before enrollment deadlines, the team can define scaling behavior for the production variant so capacity can increase during demand spikes and decrease when load falls. The relevant service behavior is described in Automatically scale Amazon SageMaker AI models and Define a scaling policy.

SageMaker Model Monitor, CloudTrail Insights, and Batch Transform solve different problems. Model Monitor focuses on data quality, model quality, bias drift, and feature attribution drift. CloudTrail is for API audit and governance, not endpoint serving performance. Batch Transform is an offline inference pattern and is not a substitute for an interactive real-time endpoint.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A professional sports league's analytics platform team hosts a player injury risk model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. Request volume is high before games and during halftime, but it drops significantly overnight. The endpoint uses a fixed instance count that was chosen months ago. The team needs to reduce unused inference capacity while maintaining low latency during traffic spikes. The team also wants to avoid manually resizing the endpoint. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A professional sports league's analytics platform team hosts a player injury risk model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. Request volume is high before games and during halftime, but it drops significantly overnight. The endpoint uses a fixed instance count that was chosen months ago. The team needs to reduce unused inference capacity while maintaining low latency during traffic spikes. The team also wants to avoid manually resizing the endpoint.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Move the model to SageMaker Serverless Inference, and rely on serverless scaling without validating cold start latency.
Create an AWS Budgets cost budget with SNS notifications, and resize the endpoint manually when alerts are received.
Run SageMaker Inference Recommender once to choose a lower cost instance type, and keep the endpoint at a fixed instance count.
Configure SageMaker automatic scaling for the endpoint variants based on CloudWatch metrics, and load test the scaling policy before rollout.

correctText: Configure SageMaker automatic scaling for the endpoint variants based on CloudWatch metrics, and load test the scaling policy before rollout.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a SageMaker real-time endpoint with predictable peaks and quiet periods, automatic scaling is the best fit because it changes the number of endpoint instances in response to traffic-related signals. CloudWatch provides the operational metrics that help you observe endpoint behavior, and scaling policies let the endpoint fleet expand or contract instead of remaining overprovisioned all day. See Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch and Automatically scale Amazon SageMaker models.

SageMaker Inference Recommender is useful when the team needs to benchmark instance types and endpoint configurations. It can inform right-sizing decisions, but a one-time recommendation does not solve a workload whose demand changes throughout the day. The service is best viewed as a way to choose better configurations, not as a replacement for runtime scaling. See Amazon SageMaker Inference Recommender.

Serverless Inference can reduce cost for intermittent workloads, but the scenario requires maintaining low latency during spikes. Because serverless endpoints can experience cold starts after idle periods, the team should not move to serverless without confirming that the latency behavior is acceptable. Inference cost optimization often involves selecting the right hosting mode, right-sizing, and scaling, not choosing the lowest-management option blindly. See Optimize inference costs in Amazon SageMaker.

AWS Budgets helps monitor and control spend by creating cost or usage budgets and sending notifications. It is a governance and alerting tool, not a traffic-aware endpoint scaling mechanism. It can complement the solution by warning about unexpected spend, but it does not replace automatic scaling for this latency and capacity problem. See Managing your costs with AWS Budgets.

questions.promptHtml: A freight rail operator's ML operations team hosts a shipment delay prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team wants to detect anomalous changes in live inference request features, identify missing or unexpected features, and receive notifications when quality deviations occur. The team wants to avoid writing custom anomaly detection code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A freight rail operator's ML operations team hosts a shipment delay prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team wants to detect anomalous changes in live inference request features, identify missing or unexpected features, and receive notifications when quality deviations occur. The team wants to avoid writing custom anomaly detection code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail Insights for SageMaker API activity, route Insights events through EventBridge, and configure SNS notifications.
Enable Data Capture on the endpoint, create a data quality baseline, schedule SageMaker Model Monitor jobs, and configure CloudWatch alarms.
Create AWS Config rules for the endpoint configuration, send noncompliance events to EventBridge, and configure SNS notifications.
Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query endpoint logs, save the queries to dashboards, and review matching error patterns.

correctText: Enable Data Capture on the endpoint, create a data quality baseline, schedule SageMaker Model Monitor jobs, and configure CloudWatch alarms.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Model Monitor is designed for operational monitoring of deployed models. For data quality monitoring, it uses a baseline from reference data and compares production inference traffic against that baseline to surface deviations such as data drift, anomalies, outliers, and changes in features. See the SageMaker documentation for Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor and Monitor data quality.

The practical workflow is to capture endpoint inputs and outputs, store the captured data in Amazon S3, run monitoring jobs on a schedule, and use CloudWatch metrics or alarms for notification. This fits an ML operations requirement because it monitors the behavior of the model's production data, not just the health of the compute infrastructure.

CloudTrail Insights, AWS Config, and CloudWatch Logs Insights solve different monitoring problems. CloudTrail focuses on API activity and auditing, AWS Config focuses on resource configuration and compliance, and CloudWatch Logs Insights helps query logs for troubleshooting. Those services are valuable in an ML platform, but they do not replace baseline-driven monitoring of inference data quality.

questions.promptHtml: An energy grid operator's forecasting team trains an Amazon SageMaker model from tens of terabytes of historical waveform files stored in Amazon S3. Jobs run repeatedly on the same dataset. The current S3 File mode setup spends too much time copying the full dataset into the training containers before training can begin. The team wants low-latency access during training and wants to avoid building its own data-copy process. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
An energy grid operator's forecasting team trains an Amazon SageMaker model from tens of terabytes of historical waveform files stored in Amazon S3. Jobs run repeatedly on the same dataset. The current S3 File mode setup spends too much time copying the full dataset into the training containers before training can begin. The team wants low-latency access during training and wants to avoid building its own data-copy process.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Configure the SageMaker training input channel to use the file system from a VPC-enabled training job.
Configure S3 File mode for the training input so each job downloads the full dataset before training.
Copy the training files into Amazon EFS before each training job and configure the job to mount the EFS file system.
Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that links the training bucket as its data repository.
Attach Amazon EBS volumes to the SageMaker notebook instance and train from those mounted volumes.

correctText: Configure the SageMaker training input channel to use the file system from a VPC-enabled training job.
Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that links the training bucket as its data repository.
questions.explanationHtml:
For large, repeatedly used training datasets, Amazon FSx for Lustre is a common fit because it provides a high-performance file system for workloads such as machine learning and can be linked to data in Amazon S3. Instead of using S3 File mode, which copies objects into the training container before training starts, the training job can mount the file system and read the data through the file system path.

SageMaker supports training data from Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, and Amazon FSx for Lustre. File system sources require the training job to have the necessary VPC networking so the training instances can mount the file system, and SageMaker exposes training channels inside the container under paths such as /opt/ml/input/data/<channel_name>. See Overview of SageMaker AI training data access options, Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as a training data source, and Link your file system to an S3 bucket.

The main tradeoff is that S3 access modes are simple and cost-effective for many workloads, but copying tens of terabytes at the start of every job can become a training bottleneck. A file system approach adds VPC and storage configuration, but it avoids repeatedly staging the entire dataset and provides lower-latency file access for demanding training workloads.
