questions.promptHtml: A biotech sequencing lab's ML operations team runs Amazon SageMaker training jobs, notebooks, and endpoints in several AWS accounts. The team has applied cost allocation tags for project and environment. Leadership wants to review monthly cost and usage trends by service and tag, create custom reports, and estimate future spend based on previous usage with the least operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A biotech sequencing lab's ML operations team runs Amazon SageMaker training jobs, notebooks, and endpoints in several AWS accounts. The team has applied cost allocation tags for project and environment. Leadership wants to review monthly cost and usage trends by service and tag, create custom reports, and estimate future spend based on previous usage with the least operational overhead.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Trusted Advisor to review cost optimization checks and export the recommendations for each account.
Use AWS Cost Explorer to filter and group cost and usage data by service and tags, and create forecasts.
Use AWS Billing and Cost Management to download invoices and manually reconcile SageMaker charges each month.
Use AWS Budgets to filter costs by service and tags, and send SNS notifications at configured thresholds.

correctText: Use AWS Cost Explorer to filter and group cost and usage data by service and tags, and create forecasts.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Cost Explorer is the best fit when the task is to analyze AWS cost and usage over time. It provides managed reporting for historical spend, lets teams create custom reports, and supports forecasting from previous usage. For an ML team that tags SageMaker resources by project and environment, this gives leadership a low-overhead way to understand where spend is going without building a custom data pipeline.

AWS Budgets is complementary, but it solves a different problem. Budgets is used to define cost or usage limits and send alerts when actual or forecasted spend approaches or exceeds those limits. It is useful for guardrails, but it is not the main tool for exploratory cost trend analysis.

AWS Trusted Advisor helps identify recommendations such as cost optimization opportunities, performance improvements, security findings, fault tolerance issues, service limit concerns, and operational excellence items. That makes it useful for optimization reviews, but not for producing tagged monthly spend trends and forecasts. Manual invoice reconciliation has the highest operational burden and should be avoided for routine ML cost monitoring.

For more information, see AWS Cost Explorer overview, AWS Budgets documentation, and AWS Trusted Advisor Recommendations documentation.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A global shipping port authority's ML platform team is deploying an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for berth congestion predictions. The inference container must call an internal feature API that is reachable only from private subnets in a VPC. The container also must load model artifacts from Amazon S3. Security policy prohibits internet access from the endpoint subnets. Which TWO actions should the team take to meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A global shipping port authority's ML platform team is deploying an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for berth congestion predictions. The inference container must call an internal feature API that is reachable only from private subnets in a VPC. The container also must load model artifacts from Amazon S3. Security policy prohibits internet access from the endpoint subnets.

Which TWO actions should the team take to meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure the SageMaker AI model deployment with VPC subnets and security groups that allow access to the internal feature API.
Configure only a SageMaker Runtime interface VPC endpoint and remove the VPC settings from the model deployment.
Create an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint, update the route tables, and allow the required bucket access through endpoint and bucket policies.
Route the endpoint subnets through a NAT gateway and send Amazon S3 and feature API traffic through the public internet.
Enable network isolation for the model container and rely on SageMaker AI to retrieve all runtime dependencies from Amazon S3.

correctText: Configure the SageMaker AI model deployment with VPC subnets and security groups that allow access to the internal feature API.
Create an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint, update the route tables, and allow the required bucket access through endpoint and bucket policies.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a SageMaker AI hosted endpoint that must reach private resources, configure the hosted model with VPC subnets and security groups. This gives the inference container network placement that can reach resources such as an internal feature API, subject to normal VPC routing and security group rules. AWS documents this pattern in SageMaker AI hosted endpoints VPC access and the VpcConfig API reference.

Because the endpoint also needs model artifacts in Amazon S3 while internet egress is prohibited, the VPC needs private access to S3. An S3 VPC endpoint, with appropriate route table, endpoint policy, and bucket policy configuration, lets the endpoint environment access S3 without relying on a NAT gateway or an internet gateway.

Do not confuse private invocation of SageMaker APIs with private network access from the model container. An interface VPC endpoint for SageMaker Runtime, described in Invoking SageMaker AI privately from a VPC, is useful when client applications need to call SageMaker privately. It does not replace configuring the hosted model's VPC access or the S3 path needed by the container.

questions.promptHtml: A regional grocery chain's personalization team maintains several models that use customer loyalty, store inventory, and recent purchase features. Different teams currently recompute the same features in separate notebooks and endpoint containers, which has produced inconsistent feature values between training and real-time recommendations. The team needs reusable feature data, low-latency access for deployed models, and batch access for recurring training jobs over historical records. Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A regional grocery chain's personalization team maintains several models that use customer loyalty, store inventory, and recent purchase features. Different teams currently recompute the same features in separate notebooks and endpoint containers, which has produced inconsistent feature values between training and real-time recommendations. The team needs reusable feature data, low-latency access for deployed models, and batch access for recurring training jobs over historical records.

Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Register each shared feature set in SageMaker Model Registry as a model package version.
Create SageMaker Feature Store feature groups with online and offline stores for the shared features.
Keep independent feature transformation code in each training notebook and endpoint container.
Store feature values in SageMaker Experiments trials and query the trials during inference.
Read live feature values from the online store and build training datasets from the offline store.

correctText: Create SageMaker Feature Store feature groups with online and offline stores for the shared features.
Read live feature values from the online store and build training datasets from the offline store.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store is intended to make engineered features reusable and consistent across the ML lifecycle. Instead of recomputing customer, store, or transaction features separately for every model, teams create feature groups that define and organize shared feature records.

The key design choice in this scenario is the use of both storage modes. The online store supports low-latency feature access for deployed models, while the offline store stores historical feature records in Amazon S3 for batch training and analysis. This split exists because inference and training have different access patterns: one needs fast point lookups, while the other usually scans or joins larger historical datasets.

SageMaker Model Registry and SageMaker Experiments are valuable MLOps tools, but they solve different problems. Model Registry manages model versions and approvals, and Experiments tracks development runs and metrics. Neither service is a substitute for a central feature repository.

For more information, see Amazon SageMaker Feature Store and Feature Store storage configurations.

questions.promptHtml: A telehealth provider's care coordination team hosts an appointment no-show prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has baseline statistics from the training dataset, and actual attendance labels arrive in Amazon S3 each night. The team needs to receive alerts when live request features drift from the baseline or when prediction quality degrades, with the least custom monitoring code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A telehealth provider's care coordination team hosts an appointment no-show prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has baseline statistics from the training dataset, and actual attendance labels arrive in Amazon S3 each night. The team needs to receive alerts when live request features drift from the baseline or when prediction quality degrades, with the least custom monitoring code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run SageMaker Clarify bias drift monitoring on the endpoint, configure CloudWatch alarms, and retrain the model when bias thresholds change.
Create CloudWatch dashboards for endpoint invocations and latency, configure alarms on high latency, and review application logs after traffic spikes.
Enable CloudTrail management event logging for SageMaker, store the trail in Amazon S3, and query endpoint API activity with Athena.
Enable Data Capture on the endpoint, create data quality and model quality monitoring schedules from baselines, and configure CloudWatch alarms on violations.

correctText: Enable Data Capture on the endpoint, create data quality and model quality monitoring schedules from baselines, and configure CloudWatch alarms on violations.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor is designed for the production monitoring concerns in this scenario. It can monitor data quality drift by comparing live inference data to a baseline, and it can monitor model quality when ground truth labels become available after predictions are made. See the SageMaker overview for the supported monitoring types in Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.

Data Capture is the practical starting point for endpoint monitoring because it records inference inputs and outputs to Amazon S3 for later analysis. Those captured records can be used for monitoring, debugging, and retraining workflows, as described in Capture data from deployed models.

CloudWatch is still part of the solution, but it is not sufficient by itself. CloudWatch endpoint metrics can tell an engineer whether an endpoint is busy, slow, or unhealthy, while Model Monitor emits monitoring results that can be used for alarms when statistical constraints or quality expectations are violated. Data quality monitoring and model quality monitoring are covered in Monitor data quality and Monitor model quality metrics.

CloudTrail and Clarify solve adjacent but different problems. CloudTrail records API activity for audit investigations, and Clarify is appropriate when the requirement is bias drift or feature attribution drift. For this scenario, the best fit is managed monitoring of both live feature distributions and prediction quality, with alerts through CloudWatch.

questions.promptHtml: A digital media archive's ML engineering team is preparing clickstream and content metadata for recommendation models. Data scientists need a visual environment to import data from Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift, inspect distributions, apply built-in and custom pandas or PySpark transformations, and run a quick check of model signal before exporting the preparation flow. Data engineers also need a separate visual ETL workflow for recurring joins, sampling, and partitioned outputs from S3, Kafka, and JDBC sources with minimal infrastructure management. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A digital media archive's ML engineering team is preparing clickstream and content metadata for recommendation models. Data scientists need a visual environment to import data from Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift, inspect distributions, apply built-in and custom pandas or PySpark transformations, and run a quick check of model signal before exporting the preparation flow. Data engineers also need a separate visual ETL workflow for recurring joins, sampling, and partitioned outputs from S3, Kafka, and JDBC sources with minimal infrastructure management.

Which TWO actions will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon QuickSight ML Insights to perform ETL transformations and prepare the training datasets.
Use AWS Glue DataBrew to create visual recipes and profile jobs for the data scientists' preparation workflow.
Use Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to explore, transform, evaluate, and export the ML data preparation flow.
Use AWS Glue Studio to create visual ETL jobs that read from the required sources and write partitioned outputs.
Use Amazon Athena workgroups to run SQL queries over S3 data and manage team query settings.

correctText: Use Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to explore, transform, evaluate, and export the ML data preparation flow.
Use AWS Glue Studio to create visual ETL jobs that read from the required sources and write partitioned outputs.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Data Wrangler is the best fit for the data scientist workflow because it is purpose-built for ML data preparation. It provides a visual interface to import, analyze, visualize, transform, and export data preparation flows, including built-in transformations and custom code paths for pandas or PySpark. See Overview of Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler and Transform data.

AWS Glue Studio is the better fit for the recurring data engineering workflow because it provides visual authoring for serverless ETL jobs. It can model data movement and transformations as a visual job graph, which is appropriate for joins, filters, schema changes, sampling, and writing curated outputs for downstream ML use. See AWS Glue Studio visual ETL jobs and AWS Glue managed transforms.

AWS Glue DataBrew is also a visual preparation service, but it is not the right choice for evaluating ML signal with a SageMaker-style quick model or exporting a SageMaker data preparation flow. Athena is useful for SQL exploration over S3, and QuickSight is useful for dashboards and visual analysis, but neither replaces a dedicated visual ETL authoring tool for the recurring pipeline requirement. For DataBrew concepts, see AWS Glue DataBrew core concepts and terms.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: An aerospace manufacturer's predictive maintenance group has a reviewed architecture for each new model project. The pattern includes a source repository, automated build and test stages, Amazon SageMaker processing and training jobs, model evaluation, registration in SageMaker Model Registry, and a separate deployment workflow for approved models. The group wants to script this pattern so new projects can be created consistently with minimal custom orchestration code and traceable CI/CD assets. Which TWO actions should the ML engineer take?
questions.promptText:
An aerospace manufacturer's predictive maintenance group has a reviewed architecture for each new model project. The pattern includes a source repository, automated build and test stages, Amazon SageMaker processing and training jobs, model evaluation, registration in SageMaker Model Registry, and a separate deployment workflow for approved models. The group wants to script this pattern so new projects can be created consistently with minimal custom orchestration code and traceable CI/CD assets.

Which TWO actions should the ML engineer take?

options.text: Create a SageMaker Project from an MLOps template to provision the repository, build, deploy, and workflow resources.
Create ECS services on Fargate for each ML lifecycle stage and scale the task count for training and deployment.
Create EventBridge rules for each lifecycle event to invoke separate SageMaker jobs and update deployments independently.
Define a SageMaker Pipeline for the processing, training, evaluation, and registration stages, and version the definition with the code.
Create a Step Functions state machine to call SageMaker jobs and manually maintain model promotion logic.

correctText: Create a SageMaker Project from an MLOps template to provision the repository, build, deploy, and workflow resources.
Define a SageMaker Pipeline for the processing, training, evaluation, and registration stages, and version the definition with the code.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Projects and SageMaker Pipelines work together for this type of requirement. A project template gives a team a repeatable MLOps scaffold, such as repositories and CI/CD resources, while a pipeline defines the actual ML workflow stages that run processing, training, evaluation, and model registration. See SageMaker MLOps project templates and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines.

The important mental model is to separate project infrastructure from workflow orchestration. Projects standardize how a new ML project is created and governed, while Pipelines captures the repeatable DAG-like ML process that can be versioned, executed, and integrated into CI/CD. EventBridge and Step Functions are useful orchestration tools in many AWS architectures, and Step Functions can call SageMaker jobs as shown in AWS Step Functions integration with SageMaker, but using them as the primary mechanism here would require more custom coordination than the stated requirement calls for. ECS on Fargate is a valid serverless container platform, but it is not the lowest-overhead way to recreate a SageMaker-centered ML lifecycle pattern.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A municipal water utility's ML platform team maintains a leakage prediction model on Amazon SageMaker. Data scientists commit preprocessing, training, and evaluation code to a Git repository. The team wants accepted changes to automatically run repeatable ML workflow steps, track model versions, and promote endpoint updates through a staged release process with minimal custom orchestration. Which solution best meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A municipal water utility's ML platform team maintains a leakage prediction model on Amazon SageMaker. Data scientists commit preprocessing, training, and evaluation code to a Git repository. The team wants accepted changes to automatically run repeatable ML workflow steps, track model versions, and promote endpoint updates through a staged release process with minimal custom orchestration.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon ECR repository and deploy the inference container with Amazon ECS on Fargate after each Git commit.
Create a SageMaker Project from an MLOps template that uses SageMaker Pipelines and CodePipeline for staged releases.
Create a SageMaker Model Registry package group and have engineers update SageMaker endpoints manually after validation.
Create a CodeBuild project that trains the model and use EventBridge schedules to update SageMaker endpoints nightly.

correctText: Create a SageMaker Project from an MLOps template that uses SageMaker Pipelines and CodePipeline for staged releases.
questions.explanationHtml:
CI/CD in ML extends normal application delivery practices to include data processing, training, evaluation, model versioning, approval, and deployment. SageMaker Projects are designed for this MLOps pattern because they standardize the development environment, connect code repositories, and create CI/CD resources around SageMaker Pipelines and deployment workflows.

SageMaker Pipelines models the ML workflow as repeatable steps, such as processing, training, evaluation, and model registration. CodePipeline and CodeBuild fit around that workflow by automating source, build, test, and release stages, which gives teams traceability and a safer promotion path from staging to production.

Model Registry alone is not enough because it is primarily a catalog and governance mechanism for model versions, not a complete workflow orchestrator. A custom CodeBuild and EventBridge solution can work for simple automation, but it requires the team to recreate MLOps capabilities that SageMaker Projects and Pipelines already provide. Deploying directly to ECS on Fargate is a valid container pattern for some applications, but it does not meet the stated need to manage SageMaker ML workflow steps with minimal custom orchestration.

For more information, see What are SageMaker AI Projects?, Amazon SageMaker Pipelines overview, and Continuous integration and continuous delivery concepts in CodePipeline.

questions.promptHtml: A public university's research computing team is creating a central repository for genomics CSV files, experiment metadata in JSON, and microscope images. Different labs will use the repository for future analytics and machine learning projects, but the access patterns and final schemas are not yet known. The team wants to minimize initial storage cost and avoid upfront data modeling while keeping the data available for later SQL based exploration. Which storage approach best meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A public university's research computing team is creating a central repository for genomics CSV files, experiment metadata in JSON, and microscope images. Different labs will use the repository for future analytics and machine learning projects, but the access patterns and final schemas are not yet known. The team wants to minimize initial storage cost and avoid upfront data modeling while keeping the data available for later SQL based exploration.

Which storage approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Place the data on Amazon EFS, mount the file system from notebooks, and organize the files by lab directory.
Load the data into Amazon Redshift tables, define the schema before ingestion, and query the data with Redshift SQL.
Import the data into Amazon FSx for Lustre, process the files from training jobs, and keep the repository on the file system.
Store the raw data in Amazon S3 as a data lake, catalog the datasets with AWS Glue, and query the data with Amazon Athena.

correctText: Store the raw data in Amazon S3 as a data lake, catalog the datasets with AWS Glue, and query the data with Amazon Athena.
questions.explanationHtml:
When the data includes a mix of structured, semi-structured, and unstructured formats, and the future analytics requirements are uncertain, an Amazon S3 data lake is typically the best initial storage decision. A data lake stores raw data in its native format and supports schema-on-read, so teams can defer modeling decisions until they understand how the data will be used.

AWS Glue can provide catalog metadata for data stored in S3, and Amazon Athena can query that data with SQL without loading it into a warehouse first. This balances cost and flexibility because the team avoids transforming every dataset into a fixed schema before there is a proven analytics need.

A warehouse such as Amazon Redshift is better when the data is already structured and the organization needs fast, repeated, complex BI queries over a known schema. File systems such as Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx for Lustre solve different problems, shared POSIX access and high performance file processing, but they are not the best default repository for a flexible analytics and ML data lake.

For additional context, see the AWS storage decision guide, the Amazon S3 storage classes documentation, and the SageMaker guidance on accessing training data from storage services.

questions.promptHtml: A property insurance carrier's actuarial ML team is selecting a model to predict claim severity from tabular policy, property, and weather features. Several candidate models meet the minimum RMSE target, but compliance reviewers require the team to understand which features influence predictions before the model is approved. The team wants to include interpretability in the model selection process without abandoning managed SageMaker workflows. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A property insurance carrier's actuarial ML team is selecting a model to predict claim severity from tabular policy, property, and weather features. Several candidate models meet the minimum RMSE target, but compliance reviewers require the team to understand which features influence predictions before the model is approved. The team wants to include interpretability in the model selection process without abandoning managed SageMaker workflows.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Choose the candidate with the lowest RMSE and defer feature contribution analysis until production monitoring begins.
Select the least complex candidate algorithm that satisfies the predefined performance and explainability requirements.
Use SageMaker Model Monitor data quality baselines as the primary method to explain each candidate model.
Compare candidate models by using SageMaker Clarify feature attribution results together with validation metrics.
Select an ensemble or deep learning model whenever it improves RMSE, regardless of the added model complexity.

correctText: Select the least complex candidate algorithm that satisfies the predefined performance and explainability requirements.
Compare candidate models by using SageMaker Clarify feature attribution results together with validation metrics.
questions.explanationHtml:
Interpretability should be considered during model and algorithm selection, not bolted on only after deployment. A practical selection process compares candidate models on the required performance metric, such as RMSE for a regression problem, and also evaluates whether the model behavior can be explained to stakeholders who must approve or use the predictions.

SageMaker Clarify helps with this tradeoff by producing feature attribution information, including SHAP-based explanations, so teams can understand how input features contribute to predictions. This is especially useful when comparing a simpler model that barely meets the target against a more complex model with a small performance gain. See Amazon SageMaker Clarify model explainability and Feature attributions that use Shapley values.

A simpler algorithm can be the better engineering choice when it meets the business performance threshold. For example, Linear Learner learns a linear function or linear threshold function for regression and classification, which can be easier to reason about than a large ensemble or deep neural network. The point is not that simple models are always best, but that accuracy versus complexity is a real model development tradeoff. See SageMaker Linear Learner algorithm.

Production monitoring and model governance artifacts are still useful later in the lifecycle, but they do not replace interpretability analysis when selecting a candidate model. If a team chooses the lowest-RMSE model without checking feature contribution and explanation quality, it can end up with a model that is difficult to audit, debug, or justify even though it performs well on validation data.

questions.promptHtml: An online education platform's learner analytics team stores raw enrollment and support-ticket exports as CSV files in Amazon S3. The team must determine which datasets contain personally identifiable information (PII) and create a sanitized S3 output for model development. Analysts need repeatable visual preparation steps that can mask, hash, or delete PII fields without writing custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
An online education platform's learner analytics team stores raw enrollment and support-ticket exports as CSV files in Amazon S3. The team must determine which datasets contain personally identifiable information (PII) and create a sanitized S3 output for model development. Analysts need repeatable visual preparation steps that can mask, hash, or delete PII fields without writing custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Lake Formation LF-Tags to classify PII columns. Grant analysts data filters that hide sensitive columns when querying catalog tables.
Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII entities in the CSV files. Redact the original files in place before analysts run data preparation jobs.
Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in S3. Use AWS Glue DataBrew profile and recipe jobs to apply PII transformations and write sanitized data to S3.
Enable AWS KMS encryption on the S3 bucket. Grant analysts access to the KMS key and require SageMaker jobs to read encrypted raw objects.

correctText: Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in S3. Use AWS Glue DataBrew profile and recipe jobs to apply PII transformations and write sanitized data to S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon Macie is designed to discover and classify sensitive data in Amazon S3, which makes it a good first step when a team needs to understand where PII exists across data lake objects. Macie helps identify sensitive data so the team can make informed decisions about which datasets need additional controls or transformation before they are used for ML.

AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool that supports PII identification and obfuscation-oriented transformations. For this scenario, a DataBrew profile job can help inspect the dataset, and a recipe job can apply actions such as masking, hashing, substitution, encryption, nulling, or deletion before writing a sanitized output to S3.

Encryption with KMS is important for protecting data, but it is not the same as anonymization or masking. Lake Formation permissions and filters are useful for governing access to cataloged data, but access control alone does not produce a reusable de-identified training dataset. Comprehend can be useful for PII detection and redaction in text, but DataBrew is the better fit when analysts need a visual, repeatable preparation workflow for tabular files.

For more information, see Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery in S3, AWS Glue DataBrew personal information protection, and AWS Lake Formation data filters.

questions.promptHtml: A live music ticketing platform's ML data engineering team receives two real-time event feeds. The purchase feed only needs lightweight per-record normalization before delivery to Amazon S3 for a training data lake, and the team does not need to replay that feed. The behavioral feed requires continuous cleansing, windowed aggregation, and enrichment by using Spark before loading curated records for downstream ML. The team wants managed AWS services and minimal custom infrastructure. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A live music ticketing platform's ML data engineering team receives two real-time event feeds. The purchase feed only needs lightweight per-record normalization before delivery to Amazon S3 for a training data lake, and the team does not need to replay that feed. The behavioral feed requires continuous cleansing, windowed aggregation, and enrichment by using Spark before loading curated records for downstream ML. The team wants managed AWS services and minimal custom infrastructure.

Which TWO actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure Amazon Data Firehose as the replayable stream buffer and run downstream transformations after rereading retained events.
Query incoming events with Amazon Athena workgroups and schedule CTAS statements to transform each stream into curated S3 files.
Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job to consume the behavioral stream and run Spark transformations before writing curated output.
Build a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow with Quick Model and use the flow as the continuous processor for both streams.
Configure Amazon Data Firehose to invoke AWS Lambda for lightweight purchase record normalization before delivering events to Amazon S3.

correctText: Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job to consume the behavioral stream and run Spark transformations before writing curated output.
Configure Amazon Data Firehose to invoke AWS Lambda for lightweight purchase record normalization before delivering events to Amazon S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon Data Firehose is a good fit when the goal is to load streaming data into a destination such as Amazon S3 with low operational overhead. It can buffer records and invoke AWS Lambda to transform incoming data before delivery, which makes it suitable for lightweight normalization such as reshaping records or converting formats. See Transform source data in Amazon Data Firehose.

For the behavioral feed, the requirement is not just per-record transformation. Continuous cleansing, enrichment, and windowed aggregation are classic streaming ETL tasks, and AWS Glue streaming ETL uses Spark-based processing patterns for this kind of managed transformation workload. The relevant documentation pages are Adding streaming ETL jobs in AWS Glue and AWS Glue streaming concepts.

Athena is excellent for SQL analysis over data in Amazon S3, especially with formats such as Parquet, but it is not a streaming transformation engine. SageMaker Data Wrangler helps ML teams visually prepare, profile, and transform data, but it is not the runtime for always-on stream processing. Firehose also should not be treated as a replayable stream buffer, because its role is managed delivery rather than durable stream retention and replay.

questions.promptText:
A pharmaceutical clinical operations team hosts an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint that predicts whether clinical trial sites will miss enrollment targets. After the team launches a new patient referral channel, engineers want alerts if production request features begin to differ statistically from the training baseline. Outcome labels are delayed by several months, and the team wants a managed approach with minimal custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor model quality monitoring, configure ground truth label ingestion, and alarm on accuracy metric deviations.
Enable CloudTrail Insights for SageMaker management events, route insights to EventBridge, and alarm on endpoint update anomalies.
Enable SageMaker Clarify bias drift monitoring, configure referral channel as a facet, and alarm on bias metric thresholds.
Enable SageMaker Model Monitor data quality monitoring, create a training-data baseline, and configure CloudWatch alarms for constraint violations.

correctText: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor data quality monitoring, create a training-data baseline, and configure CloudWatch alarms for constraint violations.
questions.explanationHtml:
Drift monitoring is most useful when you match the monitoring type to the kind of change you need to detect. In this scenario, the first signal is a change in live input features after a new referral channel is introduced, while labels arrive too late to support timely quality scoring. SageMaker Model Monitor data quality monitoring is designed for this pattern: it uses a baseline of feature statistics and constraints, compares captured production inference data against that baseline, and emits monitoring results that can be surfaced through CloudWatch alarms.

Model quality monitoring is a different control loop. It evaluates whether predictions remain accurate by comparing predictions with ground truth labels, so it is valuable when labels are available but is not the best fit for unlabeled feature drift. Clarify bias drift and feature attribution drift are also important, but they answer narrower questions about fairness metrics or changes in how features influence predictions rather than the general statistical drift described here.

CloudTrail and CloudTrail Insights help with governance and audit by recording API activity and detecting unusual management event patterns. They are not model observability tools for inference payloads. For more information, see Monitor data and model quality, bias, and feature attribution drift with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor and Monitor data quality.
